subproblems.title: Carathéodory's criterion (Simon 1.13, with Lemma 1.6)
subproblems.statement: For every metric space (X, d) and every outer measure μ on X such that μ(A ∪ B) = μ(A) + μ(B) whenever A, B ⊆ X admit a real r > 0 with r ≤ d(a, b) for all a ∈ A, b ∈ B, every Borel set E ⊆ X is μ-measurable in Carathéodory's sense (μ.IsCaratheodory E).
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `CaratheodoryCriterion` (Simon, Ch. 1, Lemma 1.6 and Theorem 1.13; printed proof, transcribed and completed).

Statement. Let (X, d) be a metric space and μ an outer measure on X with the property
  (H) μ(A ∪ B) = μ(A) + μ(B) whenever A, B ⊆ X and there is a real r > 0 with r ≤ d(a, b) for all a ∈ A, b ∈ B.
Then every Borel set E ⊆ X is μ-measurable in Carathéodory's sense (Def. 1.2): μ(S) = μ(S ∩ E) + μ(S ∖ E) for every S ⊆ X. (In Lean: `μ.IsCaratheodory E` for every `E` with `MeasurableSet[borel X] E`.)

Notation. M denotes the family of μ-measurable sets. An outer measure is monotone, countably subadditive and μ(∅) = 0 (Simon 1.1).

Step 0 (Remark 1.3). A ⊆ X is μ-measurable iff μ(S) ≥ μ(S ∖ A) + μ(S ∩ A) for every S with μ(S) < ∞. Indeed this inequality is trivial when μ(S) = ∞, and the reverse inequality μ(S) ≤ μ(S ∖ A) + μ(S ∩ A) always holds by subadditivity.

Step 1 (Lemma 1.6: M is a σ-algebra; printed Steps 1–5).
 1a. ∅, X ∈ M, and A ∈ M ⇔ X ∖ A ∈ M, because the defining identity is symmetric in A and X ∖ A.
 1b. (Printed Step 1.) A₁, A₂ ∈ M ⇒ A₂ ∖ A₁ ∈ M. Let μ(S) < ∞. Measurability of A₁ with test set S ∩ A₂ gives μ(S ∩ A₂) = μ(S ∩ A₂ ∩ A₁) + μ(S ∩ (A₂ ∖ A₁)); measurability of A₂ with test set S gives μ(S) = μ(S ∩ A₂) + μ(S ∖ A₂). All terms are finite, so
   μ(S ∩ (A₂ ∖ A₁)) = μ(S) − μ(S ∖ A₂) − μ(S ∩ A₂ ∩ A₁) ≤ μ(S) − μ((S ∖ A₂) ∪ (S ∩ A₂ ∩ A₁)) = μ(S) − μ(S ∖ (A₂ ∖ A₁)),
   using subadditivity and the identity (S ∖ A₂) ∪ (S ∩ A₂ ∩ A₁) = (S ∖ A₂) ∪ (S ∩ A₁) = S ∖ (A₂ ∖ A₁). By Step 0, A₂ ∖ A₁ ∈ M.
 1c. (Printed Step 2.) A₁, A₂ ∈ M ⇒ A₁ ∪ A₂ ∈ M: by 1a and 1b, (X ∖ A₁) ∩ (X ∖ A₂) = (X ∖ A₂) ∖ A₁ ∈ M, hence A₁ ∪ A₂ = X ∖ ((X ∖ A₁) ∩ (X ∖ A₂)) ∈ M. If A₁, A₂ ∈ M are disjoint, then using A₁ with test set S ∩ (A₁ ∪ A₂): μ(S ∩ (A₁ ∪ A₂)) = μ(S ∩ A₁) + μ(S ∩ A₂).
 1d. (Printed Step 3.) By induction, finite unions of members of M lie in M, and μ(S ∩ ⋃_{j≤N} A_j) = Σ_{j≤N} μ(S ∩ A_j) for pairwise disjoint A₁, …, A_N ∈ M and every S.
 1e. (Printed Step 4.) If A₁, A₂, … ∈ M are pairwise disjoint and S ⊆ X, then by 1d and monotonicity
   μ(S) = μ(S ∩ ⋃_{j≤N} A_j) + μ(S ∖ ⋃_{j≤N} A_j) ≥ Σ_{j≤N} μ(S ∩ A_j) + μ(S ∖ ⋃_{j≥1} A_j).
   Letting N → ∞ and using subadditivity, μ(S) ≥ Σ_j μ(S ∩ A_j) + μ(S ∖ ⋃_j A_j) ≥ μ(S ∩ ⋃_j A_j) + μ(S ∖ ⋃_j A_j); by Step 0, ⋃_j A_j ∈ M. (Replacing S by S ∩ ⋃_j A_j also gives μ(S ∩ ⋃_j A_j) = Σ_j μ(S ∩ A_j), Remark 1.7.)
 1f. (Printed Step 5.) For arbitrary A₁, A₂, … ∈ M put Ã_j := A_j ∖ (A₁ ∪ ⋯ ∪ A_{j−1}) ∈ M (1b, 1d). The Ã_j are pairwise disjoint with ⋃_j Ã_j = ⋃_j A_j, so ⋃_j A_j ∈ M by 1e.
 Hence M is a σ-algebra.

Step 2 (reduction to closed sets). The Borel σ-algebra is the smallest σ-algebra containing the open sets, equivalently (by closure under complements) the closed sets. Since M is a σ-algebra (Step 1), it suffices to show that every closed set C ⊆ X lies in M. If C = ∅ this is clear, so let C ≠ ∅. Then dist(x, C) := inf_{c∈C} d(x, c) is a finite, 1-Lipschitz function of x, and, C being closed, dist(x, C) = 0 ⇔ x ∈ C. By Step 0 we must show
  (*) μ(S) ≥ μ(S ∖ C) + μ(S ∩ C) for every S ⊆ X with μ(S) < ∞.

Step 3. For j ≥ 1 let C_j := {x ∈ X : dist(x, C) ≤ 1/j}. If a ∈ S ∖ C_j and b ∈ S ∩ C, then d(a, b) ≥ dist(a, C) > 1/j, so (H) applies with r = 1/j and, by monotonicity,
  μ(S) ≥ μ((S ∖ C_j) ∪ (S ∩ C)) = μ(S ∖ C_j) + μ(S ∩ C).
Thus (*) follows once we show lim_{j→∞} μ(S ∖ C_j) = μ(S ∖ C).

Step 4. For k ≥ 1 let R_k := {x ∈ S : 1/(k+1) < dist(x, C) ≤ 1/k}. Since C is closed, S ∖ C = {x ∈ S : dist(x, C) > 0} = (S ∖ C_j) ∪ ⋃_{k≥j} R_k for every j. By monotonicity and subadditivity,
  μ(S ∖ C_j) ≤ μ(S ∖ C) ≤ μ(S ∖ C_j) + Σ_{k≥j} μ(R_k).
Hence it suffices to show Σ_{k≥1} μ(R_k) < ∞ (then the tails tend to 0).

Step 5. If i ≥ 1, l ≥ i + 2, x ∈ R_i and y ∈ R_l, then, dist(·, C) being 1-Lipschitz,
  d(x, y) ≥ dist(x, C) − dist(y, C) > 1/(i+1) − 1/l ≥ 1/(i+1) − 1/(i+2) > 0.
Consequently, for N ≥ 2 the sets ⋃_{k=1}^{N−1} R_{2k} and R_{2N} satisfy the hypothesis of (H) with r := 1/(2N−1) − 1/(2N) > 0 (for k ≤ N − 1: 1/(2k+1) − 1/(2N) ≥ r), and likewise ⋃_{k=1}^{N−1} R_{2k−1} and R_{2N−1} with r := 1/(2N−2) − 1/(2N−1) > 0. By (H) and induction on N,
  Σ_{k=1}^N μ(R_{2k}) = μ(⋃_{k=1}^N R_{2k}) ≤ μ(S),   Σ_{k=1}^N μ(R_{2k−1}) = μ(⋃_{k=1}^N R_{2k−1}) ≤ μ(S).
Letting N → ∞, Σ_{k≥1} μ(R_k) ≤ 2μ(S) < ∞.

Step 6 (conclusion). By Steps 4–5, μ(S ∖ C_j) → μ(S ∖ C); letting j → ∞ in Step 3 gives (*). So every closed set is μ-measurable, and by Step 2 every Borel set is μ-measurable. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding; not part of the argument): Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.OuterMeasure.IsMetric.borel_le_caratheodory` (Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Hausdorff.lean) is this theorem for the hypothesis `μ.IsMetric` (additivity on `Metric.AreSeparated` pairs); SimonGMT wraps it as `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.caratheodory_metric_criterion`. The only bridge needed is: `Metric.AreSeparated A B` (some r ∈ ℝ≥0∞, r ≠ 0, with r ≤ edist a b) yields the real r' := (min r 1).toReal > 0 with r' ≤ dist a b, so (H) implies `μ.IsMetric`.
proof_key_steps: Lemma 1.6: the Carathéodory-measurable sets form a σ-algebra (printed Steps 1–5).
Reduce to nonempty closed C and, by Remark 1.3, to μ(S) ≥ μ(S ∖ C) + μ(S ∩ C) for μ(S) < ∞.
With C_j = {dist(·, C) ≤ 1/j}, the sets S ∖ C_j and S ∩ C are 1/j-separated, so μ(S) ≥ μ(S ∖ C_j) + μ(S ∩ C).
S ∖ C = (S ∖ C_j) ∪ ⋃_{k≥j} R_k with annuli R_k, so μ(S ∖ C_j) ≤ μ(S ∖ C) ≤ μ(S ∖ C_j) + Σ_{k≥j} μ(R_k).
R_i and R_l are positively separated for l ≥ i + 2; the hypothesis on even and odd unions gives Σ_k μ(R_k) ≤ 2μ(S) < ∞.
Hence μ(S ∖ C_j) → μ(S ∖ C): closed sets, and therefore all Borel sets, are μ-measurable.

subproblems.title: Outer and inner regularity of open σ-finite Borel-regular measures (Simon 1.15)
subproblems.statement: For every topological space X in which every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets, and every outer measure μ on X that is Borel regular and open σ-finite (X = ⋃ V_n, V_n open, μ(V_n) < ∞): (1) μ(A) = inf{μ(U) : U ⊇ A open} for every A ⊆ X, and (2) μ(A) = sup{μ(C) : C ⊆ A closed} for every μ-measurable A ⊆ X.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `BorelRegularApproximation` (Simon, Ch. 1, Theorem 1.15; printed proof, transcribed and completed).

Statement. Let X be a topological space in which every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets, and let μ be an outer measure on X which is
 • Borel regular: every Borel set is μ-measurable, and every A ⊆ X has a Borel B ⊇ A with μ(B) = μ(A); and
 • open σ-finite (Def. 1.14): X = ⋃_{n} V_n with V_n open and μ(V_n) < ∞.
Then (1) μ(A) = inf{μ(U) : U open, U ⊇ A} for every A ⊆ X, and (2) μ(A) = sup{μ(C) : C closed, C ⊆ A} for every μ-measurable A ⊆ X.

Standard facts used (Carathéodory; Simon Lemma 1.6, Remark 1.7, (1.8), (1.9)): the μ-measurable sets form a σ-algebra M containing every μ-null set; μ is countably additive on M; for an increasing sequence in M, μ(⋃) = lim μ; for a decreasing sequence in M with finite first term, μ(⋂) = lim μ. In particular μ(U ∖ A) = μ(U) − μ(A) when A ⊆ U, A ∈ M, μ(A) < ∞.

Trivial halves. By monotonicity, inf{μ(U) : U ⊇ A open} ≥ μ(A) and sup{μ(C) : C ⊆ A closed} ≤ μ(A). Only the reverse inequalities need proof.

Step 0 (restriction to a Borel set; cf. the remarks after (1.12)). Let Y ⊆ X be Borel and μ⌞Y(A) := μ(Y ∩ A).
 (a) Every μ-measurable E is μ⌞Y-measurable: for S ⊆ X, μ⌞Y(S) = μ(S ∩ Y) = μ(S ∩ Y ∩ E) + μ((S ∩ Y) ∖ E) = μ⌞Y(S ∩ E) + μ⌞Y(S ∖ E).
 (b) μ⌞Y is Borel regular: Borel sets are μ⌞Y-measurable by (a); given A, take a Borel B₃ ⊇ A ∩ Y with μ(B₃) = μ(A ∩ Y); then B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ Y) is Borel, B ⊇ A, and μ⌞Y(B) = μ(Y ∩ B₃) ≤ μ(B₃) = μ⌞Y(A).

PART I: the case μ(X) < ∞.

I.1 It suffices to prove (1) for Borel A: for arbitrary A choose a Borel B ⊇ A with μ(B) = μ(A); every open U ⊇ B contains A, so inf_{U⊇A} μ(U) ≤ inf_{U⊇B} μ(U) = μ(B) = μ(A).

I.2 For a Borel set A (finite case), (1) holds iff for every ε > 0 there is an open U ⊇ A with μ(U ∖ A) < ε (because μ(U) = μ(A) + μ(U ∖ A)). Let 𝒜 be the family of Borel sets A with this property. Every open set belongs to 𝒜 (take U = A).

I.3 𝒜 is closed under countable unions. Let A_j ∈ 𝒜 (j ≥ 1), ε > 0, and choose open U_j ⊇ A_j with μ(U_j ∖ A_j) < 2^{−j−1}ε. Then U := ⋃_j U_j is open, contains ⋃_k A_k, and U ∖ ⋃_k A_k ⊆ ⋃_j (U_j ∖ A_j), so μ(U ∖ ⋃_k A_k) ≤ ε/2 < ε.

I.4 𝒜 is closed under countable intersections. Let A_k ∈ 𝒜, A := ⋂_k A_k, ε > 0, and U_k as in I.3. Then (⋂_j U_j) ∖ A ⊆ ⋃_k (U_k ∖ A_k) (a point of ⋂_j U_j outside A lies outside some A_k but inside U_k), so μ((⋂_j U_j) ∖ A) ≤ ε/2. The Borel sets W_N := (U₁ ∩ ⋯ ∩ U_N) ∖ A decrease to (⋂_j U_j) ∖ A and μ(W₁) ≤ μ(X) < ∞, so by (1.9) μ(W_N) → μ((⋂_j U_j) ∖ A) ≤ ε/2. Hence for some N, U₁ ∩ ⋯ ∩ U_N is an open set containing A with μ((U₁ ∩ ⋯ ∩ U_N) ∖ A) < ε.

I.5 Every closed C belongs to 𝒜: by hypothesis C = ⋂_j G_j with G_j open, G_j ∈ 𝒜 (I.2), so C ∈ 𝒜 by I.4.

I.6 𝒜 contains every Borel set. Let 𝒜̃ := {A ∈ 𝒜 : X ∖ A ∈ 𝒜}. Then ∅, X ∈ 𝒜̃ (both are open and closed), 𝒜̃ is closed under complements by definition, and if A_j ∈ 𝒜̃ then ⋃_j A_j ∈ 𝒜 (I.3) and X ∖ ⋃_j A_j = ⋂_j (X ∖ A_j) ∈ 𝒜 (I.4), so ⋃_j A_j ∈ 𝒜̃. Thus 𝒜̃ is a σ-algebra. If C is closed then C ∈ 𝒜 (I.5) and X ∖ C ∈ 𝒜 (open), so C ∈ 𝒜̃. Since the Borel σ-algebra is generated by the closed sets, 𝒜̃ contains all Borel sets, hence so does 𝒜. With I.1 and I.2 this proves (1) in the finite case.

I.7 Proof of (2) in the finite case. Let A be μ-measurable and ε > 0. Apply (1) to X ∖ A: there is an open U ⊇ X ∖ A with μ(U) < μ(X ∖ A) + ε; since X ∖ A ∈ M has finite measure, μ(U ∖ (X ∖ A)) = μ(U) − μ(X ∖ A) < ε. Then C := X ∖ U is closed, C ⊆ A, and A ∖ C = A ∩ U = U ∖ (X ∖ A), so μ(A) = μ(C) + μ(A ∖ C) < μ(C) + ε (C is Borel, hence in M). Thus sup_{C⊆A closed} μ(C) ≥ μ(A).

PART II: the general (open σ-finite) case.

For each j put μ_j := μ⌞V_j. V_j is open, hence Borel, so by Step 0 μ_j is Borel regular and every μ-measurable set is μ_j-measurable; moreover μ_j(X) = μ(V_j) < ∞. The topological hypothesis on X is unchanged, so Part I applies to each μ_j.

II.1 Proof of (1). Let A ⊆ X and ε > 0; if μ(A) = ∞ there is nothing to prove (take U = X). Choose a Borel B ⊇ A with μ(B) = μ(A). By Part I (I.6, applied to μ_j and the Borel set B) there are open U_j ⊇ B with μ_j(U_j ∖ B) = μ(V_j ∩ U_j ∖ B) < 2^{−j−1}ε. Then U := ⋃_j (U_j ∩ V_j) is open; it contains B, since each x ∈ B lies in some V_j and in U_j; and U ∖ B ⊆ ⋃_j ((U_j ∩ V_j) ∖ B), so μ(U ∖ B) < ε. Hence μ(U) ≤ μ(B) + μ(U ∖ B) < μ(A) + ε, proving (1).

II.2 Proof of (2). Let A be μ-measurable and ε > 0. A is μ_j-measurable, so by I.7 for μ_j there is a closed C_j ⊆ A with μ_j(A ∖ C_j) = μ(V_j ∩ A ∖ C_j) < 2^{−j−1}ε. Since X = ⋃_j V_j,
  A ∖ ⋃_k C_k = ⋃_j (V_j ∩ A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) ⊆ ⋃_j (V_j ∩ A ∖ C_j), hence μ(A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) < ε.
Let D_N := C₁ ∪ ⋯ ∪ C_N: a closed subset of A; the D_N increase and lie in M.
 • If μ(A) = ∞: μ(A) ≤ μ(⋃_k C_k) + μ(A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) forces μ(⋃_k C_k) = ∞, and by (1.8) μ(D_N) → μ(⋃_k C_k) = ∞; so sup_{C⊆A closed} μ(C) = ∞ = μ(A).
 • If μ(A) < ∞: the sets A ∖ D_N ∈ M decrease to A ∖ ⋃_k C_k and have finite measure, so by (1.9) μ(A ∖ D_N) → μ(A ∖ ⋃_k C_k) < ε; for large N, μ(D_N) = μ(A) − μ(A ∖ D_N) > μ(A) − ε.
In both cases sup_{C⊆A closed} μ(C) ≥ μ(A), proving (2). ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.IsBorelRegularOuterMeasure.simon_theorem_1_15` (Chapter01/ExactRegularity.lean) proves exactly (1) ∧ (2) under `IsBorelRegularOuterMeasure μ`, `IsOpenSigmaFinite μ` and `ClosedSetsAreGDelta X` (= ∀ ⦃C⦄, IsClosed C → IsGδ C, unfolded by `closedSetsAreGDelta_iff`); `IsCaratheodoryMeasurable μ A` is an abbreviation of `μ.IsCaratheodory A`.
proof_key_steps: Restriction to a Borel set Y: μ⌞Y is Borel regular and every μ-measurable set is μ⌞Y-measurable.
Finite case: reduce (1) to Borel A via Borel hulls; let 𝒜 be the Borel sets approximable from outside by open sets up to ε.
𝒜 contains the open sets and is closed under countable unions and (via finite intersections and continuity from above) countable intersections, so it contains the closed (G_δ) sets.
𝒜̃ = {A ∈ 𝒜 : X ∖ A ∈ 𝒜} is a σ-algebra containing the closed sets, so 𝒜 contains all Borel sets: (1) holds in the finite case.
(2) in the finite case follows by applying (1) to X ∖ A.
General case: apply the finite case to μ⌞V_j with errors 2^{−j−1}ε and recombine; in (2) treat μ(A) = ∞ and μ(A) < ∞ separately via (1.8), (1.9).

subproblems.title: Lusin's theorem (Simon 1.17)
subproblems.statement: For every topological space X in which every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets, every Borel regular outer measure μ on X, every μ-measurable A ⊆ X with μ(A) < ∞, every f : A → ℝ measurable for the trace on A of the σ-algebra of μ-measurable sets, and every real ε > 0, there is a closed C ⊆ X with C ⊆ A, μ(A ∖ C) < ε, and f restricted to C continuous.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `LusinTheorem` (Simon, Ch. 1, Theorem 1.17; printed proof, transcribed and completed).

Statement. Let X be a topological space in which every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets, μ a Borel regular outer measure on X (no σ-finiteness assumed), A ⊆ X μ-measurable with μ(A) < ∞, and f : A → ℝ measurable with respect to the trace σ-algebra {A ∩ E : E μ-measurable} on A (Borel σ-algebra on ℝ). Then for each real ε > 0 there is a closed set C ⊆ X with C ⊆ A, μ(A ∖ C) < ε, and f|_C continuous (i.e. f ∘ (inclusion C ↪ A) : C → ℝ is continuous for the subspace topology of C).

Standard facts (Carathéodory; Simon 1.6, 1.7, 1.9): the μ-measurable sets form a σ-algebra M on which μ is countably additive; decreasing sequences in M of finite measure satisfy μ(⋂) = lim μ.

Dependency. Theorem 1.15 = sibling `borel_regular_approximation` (Lean: `Submission.borel_regular_approximation : BorelRegularApproximation`).

Step 0 (measurability of level sets). For a Borel set G ⊆ ℝ, f^{−1}(G) = A ∩ E for some μ-measurable E, so f^{−1}(G), viewed as a subset of X, lies in M (A ∈ M and M is a σ-algebra).

Step 1 (remarks after (1.12): μ⌞A is Borel regular). Put μ_A(S) := μ(A ∩ S).
 (a) Every μ-measurable set is μ_A-measurable: μ_A(S) = μ(S ∩ A) = μ(S ∩ A ∩ E) + μ((S ∩ A) ∖ E) = μ_A(S ∩ E) + μ_A(S ∖ E) for E ∈ M.
 (b) Borel hulls: choose a Borel B₁ ⊇ A with μ(B₁) = μ(A); since A ∈ M and μ(A) < ∞, μ(B₁ ∖ A) = μ(B₁) − μ(A) = 0; choose a Borel B₂ ⊇ B₁ ∖ A with μ(B₂) = μ(B₁ ∖ A) = 0. Given S ⊆ X choose a Borel B₃ ⊇ S ∩ A with μ(B₃) = μ(S ∩ A). Then
   S ⊆ (S ∩ A) ∪ (X ∖ A) ⊆ B₃ ∪ (X ∖ B₁) ∪ (B₁ ∖ A) ⊆ B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ B₁) ∪ B₂,
  B is Borel, and μ_A(B) = μ(A ∩ B) ≤ μ(B₃) + μ(A ∖ B₁) + μ(B₂) = μ(B₃) + 0 + 0 = μ_A(S) (A ∖ B₁ = ∅). With (a) this shows μ_A is Borel regular.
 (c) μ_A(X) = μ(A) < ∞, so μ_A is open σ-finite (V_n := X).

Step 2 (closed inner approximation). By Theorem 1.15(2) (sibling) applied to μ_A on X: for every μ_A-measurable E, μ_A(E) = sup{μ_A(C) : C closed ⊆ E}. Consequently: if E ⊆ A is μ-measurable and η > 0, there is a closed C ⊆ E with μ(E ∖ C) < η. Indeed choose closed C ⊆ E with μ_A(C) > μ_A(E) − η (μ_A(E) = μ(E) < ∞); C is Borel, hence μ_A-measurable, so μ_A(E ∖ C) = μ_A(E) − μ_A(C) < η, and μ_A(E ∖ C) = μ(A ∩ (E ∖ C)) = μ(E ∖ C) because E ⊆ A.

Step 3 (printed construction). For i = 1, 2, … and j ∈ ℤ let A_ij := f^{−1}([(j−1)/i, j/i)) ⊆ A. By Step 0, A_ij ∈ M; for fixed i the sets A_ij (j ∈ ℤ) are pairwise disjoint with union A. By Step 2 choose closed C_ij ⊆ A_ij with μ(A_ij ∖ C_ij) < 2^{−i−|j|−2} ε. Then A ∖ ⋃_{l∈ℤ} C_il ⊆ ⋃_j (A_ij ∖ C_ij), so
  μ(A ∖ ⋃_l C_il) ≤ Σ_{j∈ℤ} 2^{−i−|j|−2} ε = (3/4)·2^{−i} ε < 2^{−i} ε.
The sets A ∖ ⋃_{|l|≤J} C_il (J = 0, 1, 2, …) belong to M, decrease to A ∖ ⋃_l C_il, and have finite measure; by (1.9) there is J(i) with
  μ(A ∖ ⋃_{|j|≤J(i)} C_ij) < 2^{−i} ε.

Step 4 (the closed set C). Let D_i := ⋃_{|j|≤J(i)} C_ij (closed, ⊆ A) and C := ⋂_{i≥1} D_i. Then C is closed, C ⊆ A, and A ∖ C = ⋃_i (A ∖ D_i), so
  μ(A ∖ C) ≤ Σ_i μ(A ∖ D_i) ≤ μ(A ∖ D₁) + Σ_{i≥2} 2^{−i} ε < 2^{−1}ε + 2^{−1}ε = ε.
In the formal statement the bound is μ(A ∖ C) < ENNReal.ofReal ε, which is the same since ε > 0.

Step 5 (continuity). For each i define g_i : D_i → ℝ by g_i := (j−1)/i on C_ij (|j| ≤ J(i)); this is well defined because the C_ij are pairwise disjoint. The finitely many sets C_ij (|j| ≤ J(i)) are closed and pairwise disjoint, so each is relatively open in D_i (its complement in D_i is a finite union of closed sets); hence g_i is locally constant and therefore continuous on D_i, and so g_i|_C is continuous. For x ∈ C and every i we have x ∈ C_ij ⊆ A_ij for some j, hence (j−1)/i ≤ f(x) < j/i, i.e. 0 ≤ f(x) − g_i(x) < 1/i. Thus g_i|_C → f|_C uniformly on C, and a uniform limit of continuous real functions is continuous. So f|_C, i.e. f ∘ inclusion(C ⊆ A), is continuous. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.IsBorelRegularOuterMeasure.simon_theorem_1_17` (Chapter01/Lusin.lean) states exactly this with `ε : ℝ≥0∞`, `ε ≠ 0` (use `ENNReal.ofReal ε`, nonzero for ε > 0), hypothesis `ClosedSetsAreGDelta X`, the subtype σ-algebra `Subtype.instMeasurableSpace` over `μ.caratheodory` (definitionally the comap), and continuity of `fun x : C => f ⟨x.1, hCA x.2⟩`, which is `f ∘ Set.inclusion hCA`.
proof_key_steps: Preimages f^{−1}(G) of Borel sets are μ-measurable subsets of A.
μ⌞A is Borel regular (Borel hulls B₁, B₂, B₃) and finite, hence open σ-finite.
Theorem 1.15(2) for μ⌞A: every μ-measurable E ⊆ A contains a closed C with μ(E ∖ C) < η.
Closed C_ij ⊆ A_ij = f^{−1}[(j−1)/i, j/i) with μ(A_ij ∖ C_ij) < 2^{−i−|j|−2}ε, and a finite truncation |j| ≤ J(i) by continuity from above.
C := ⋂_i ⋃_{|j|≤J(i)} C_ij is closed, C ⊆ A, and μ(A ∖ C) < ε.
Step functions g_i, continuous on finite disjoint closed unions, converge uniformly to f on C, so f|_C is continuous.

subproblems.title: Lⁿ = Hⁿ = Hⁿ_δ on ℝⁿ and the isodiametric inequality (Simon 2.9, 2.10)
subproblems.statement: For every n ∈ ℕ, every real δ > 0 and every A ⊆ ℝⁿ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n): Lⁿ(A) = Hⁿ(A) and Hⁿ(A) = Hⁿ_δ(A), where Lⁿ is Lebesgue outer measure and Hⁿ, Hⁿ_δ are Simon's normalized Hausdorff measure and size-δ approximation (2.1), (2.2); and for every n ∈ ℕ and A ⊆ ℝⁿ: Lⁿ(A) ≤ ω_n (diam A / 2)ⁿ with ω_n = π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2 + 1).
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `LebesgueEqHausdorff ∧ IsodiametricInequality` (Simon, Ch. 1, Theorems 2.9 and 2.10; printed proofs, transcribed and completed).

Statements. Let n ∈ ℕ and ℝⁿ := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) with the Euclidean metric.
 (2.10) For every A ⊆ ℝⁿ: Lⁿ(A) ≤ ω_n (diam A / 2)ⁿ.
 (2.9) For every real δ > 0 and every A ⊆ ℝⁿ: Lⁿ(A) = Hⁿ(A) and Hⁿ(A) = Hⁿ_δ(A).

Notation and conventions.
 • Lⁿ is Lebesgue outer measure on ℝⁿ (Lean: `volume`, Lebesgue measure on EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) evaluated on arbitrary sets, i.e. Lⁿ(A) = inf{Lⁿ(B) : B ⊇ A Borel}); it agrees with Simon's (2.7) (inf of Σ|I_j| over countable covers by open boxes) and satisfies (2.8): Lⁿ(I) = |I| for boxes and Lⁿ(A) = inf{Lⁿ(U) : U ⊇ A open}. Boundaries of boxes/cubes are Lⁿ-null.
 • ω_n := π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2 + 1) ∈ (0, ∞); it is the volume of the unit ball of ℝⁿ, and Lⁿ(B_r(x)) = ω_n rⁿ for open and for closed balls of radius r ≥ 0.
 • diam takes values in [0, ∞] (∞ for unbounded sets); x⁰ = 1 for all x ∈ [0, ∞].
 • For δ ∈ (0, ∞], Hⁿ_δ(∅) = 0 and for A ≠ ∅, Hⁿ_δ(A) = ω_n inf{Σ_j (diam C_j/2)ⁿ : A ⊆ ⋃_j C_j, C_j countably many, diam C_j < δ} (empty C_j contribute 0; inf ∅ = ∞) (2.2); Hⁿ_δ is an outer measure, non-increasing in δ, and Hⁿ := sup_{δ>0} Hⁿ_δ (2.1). Since Hⁿ_∞ ≤ Hⁿ_δ for every real δ > 0, Hⁿ(A) = sup_{real δ>0} Hⁿ_δ(A) = lim_{δ↓0} Hⁿ_δ(A). In the Lean statement δ enters as `ENNReal.ofReal δ`.

PART 0: n = 0. ℝ⁰ = {0} and L⁰ is the unit point mass (L⁰({0}) = 1, L⁰(∅) = 0); ω_0 = π⁰/Γ(1) = 1. For every δ ∈ (0, ∞]: H⁰_δ({0}) = 1, because the one-set cover {0} (diameter 0 < δ) costs ω_0·(0/2)⁰ = 1, while every cover of {0} contains a nonempty set and each nonempty set costs (diam/2)⁰ = 1. Hence L⁰ = H⁰_δ = H⁰ on both subsets of ℝ⁰, and L⁰(A) ≤ 1 = ω_0 (diam A/2)⁰. Both statements hold for n = 0. From now on n ≥ 1.

PART A: the isodiametric inequality (2.10), n ≥ 1.

A.1 Reductions. If A = ∅ the claim is trivial. If diam A = ∞ the right side is ω_n · ∞ = ∞. Otherwise A is bounded and nonempty; its closure Ā is compact (Heine–Borel), diam Ā = diam A, and Lⁿ(A) ≤ Lⁿ(Ā). So it suffices to treat nonempty compact A.

A.2 Steiner symmetrization (printed definition). Fix j ∈ {1, …, n}; let P_j := {x : x^j = 0}. For ξ ∈ P_j let ℓ_j(ξ) := {ξ + t e_j : t ∈ ℝ} and π(ξ + t e_j) := t. For compact A put A_ξ := π(A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ)) ⊆ ℝ (compact), λ(ξ) := L¹(A_ξ), and σ_j(A, ξ) := {ξ + t e_j : |t| ≤ λ(ξ)/2}. Define
  S_j(A) := ⋃{σ_j(A, ξ) : ξ ∈ P_j, A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ) ≠ ∅}.

A.3 (Printed Note: upper semicontinuity.) Let ξ ∈ P_j, η > 0 and ξ_k → ξ in P_j. Choose an open O ⊆ ℝ with A_ξ ⊆ O and L¹(O) ≤ λ(ξ) + η (outer regularity of L¹; O = ∅ if A_ξ = ∅). The set Õ := {x : x^j ∈ O} is open and contains A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ). For all large k, A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ_k) ⊆ Õ: otherwise there are k_m → ∞ and a_m ∈ (A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ_{k_m})) ∖ Õ, a subsequence converges to some a ∈ A ∖ Õ (A compact, ℝⁿ ∖ Õ closed), and a ∈ ℓ_j(ξ) because the projection of a_m onto P_j is ξ_{k_m} → ξ — contradicting A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ) ⊆ Õ. Hence A_{ξ_k} ⊆ O and λ(ξ_k) ≤ λ(ξ) + η for all large k. The same compactness argument shows: if A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ_k) ≠ ∅ for infinitely many k, then A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ) ≠ ∅.

A.4 S_j(A) is compact. If A ⊆ B_R(0) then A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ) ≠ ∅ only for |ξ| ≤ R and λ(ξ) ≤ 2R, so S_j(A) ⊆ {ξ + t e_j : |ξ| ≤ R, |t| ≤ R} is bounded. If x_k = ξ_k + t_k e_j ∈ S_j(A) converge to x = ξ + t e_j, then ξ_k → ξ, t_k → t, A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ) ≠ ∅ (A.3), and |t| = lim |t_k| ≤ limsup λ(ξ_k)/2 ≤ λ(ξ)/2 (A.3); so x ∈ σ_j(A, ξ) ⊆ S_j(A). Thus S_j(A) is closed and bounded, hence compact.

A.5 Lⁿ(S_j(A)) = Lⁿ(A). Both sets are compact, hence Borel. Identify ℝⁿ with P_j × ℝ via ξ + t e_j ↔ (ξ, t), so that Lⁿ = L^{n−1} ⊗ L¹. By Fubini–Tonelli, Lⁿ(A) = ∫_{P_j} L¹(A_ξ) dξ = ∫_{P_j} λ(ξ) dξ and Lⁿ(S_j(A)) = ∫_{P_j} L¹([−λ(ξ)/2, λ(ξ)/2]) dξ = ∫_{P_j} λ(ξ) dξ (both slices are empty/null when A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ) = ∅).

A.6 diam S_j(A) ≤ diam A (asserted in the printed text; proof). Let x = ξ + s e_j and y = η + t e_j be points of S_j(A), so A_ξ, A_η are nonempty compact, |s| ≤ λ(ξ)/2, |t| ≤ λ(η)/2. Let p⁻ := min A_ξ, p⁺ := max A_ξ, q⁻ := min A_η, q⁺ := max A_η. Then λ(ξ) ≤ p⁺ − p⁻ and λ(η) ≤ q⁺ − q⁻, so
  |s − t| ≤ |s| + |t| ≤ ½(p⁺ − p⁻) + ½(q⁺ − q⁻) = ½[(p⁺ − q⁻) + (q⁺ − p⁻)] ≤ m := max(|p⁺ − q⁻|, |q⁺ − p⁻|).
Since ξ − η ⊥ e_j and the points ξ + p^± e_j, η + q^± e_j lie in A,
  |x − y|² = |ξ − η|² + |s − t|² ≤ |ξ − η|² + m² = max(|(ξ + p⁺e_j) − (η + q⁻e_j)|², |(η + q⁺e_j) − (ξ + p⁻e_j)|²) ≤ (diam A)².

A.7 Symmetry. Let R_i(x) := x − 2x^i e_i (reflection in {x^i = 0}). By construction S_j(A) is R_j-invariant. If i ≠ j and R_i(A) = A, then S_j(A) is R_i-invariant: R_i maps P_j onto itself and ℓ_j(ξ) onto ℓ_j(R_i ξ) preserving the coordinate t, so A_{R_iξ} = π(R_i(A ∩ ℓ_j(ξ))) = A_ξ, λ(R_i ξ) = λ(ξ), and R_i(σ_j(A, ξ)) = σ_j(A, R_i ξ).

A.8 Conclusion of (2.10). Let Ã := S_n(S_{n−1}(⋯ S_1(A) ⋯)). By A.4–A.7 (inductively, the k-th set is invariant under R_1, …, R_k), Ã is a nonempty compact set with Lⁿ(Ã) = Lⁿ(A), diam Ã ≤ diam A, invariant under R_1, …, R_n and hence under x ↦ −x = R_1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ R_n. For x ∈ Ã also −x ∈ Ã, so 2|x| = |x − (−x)| ≤ diam Ã; thus Ã ⊆ B_{diam Ã/2}(0) (closed ball) and
  Lⁿ(A) = Lⁿ(Ã) ≤ ω_n (diam Ã/2)ⁿ ≤ ω_n (diam A/2)ⁿ.

PART B: Theorem 2.9, n ≥ 1, δ ∈ (0, ∞) real.

B.1 (printed “Completion of the proof of 2.9”) Lⁿ(A) ≤ Hⁿ_δ(A). If {C_j} is a countable cover of A with diam C_j < δ, then by countable subadditivity and (2.10), Lⁿ(A) ≤ Σ_j Lⁿ(C_j) ≤ Σ_j ω_n (diam C_j/2)ⁿ. Taking the infimum over such covers (if there is none, Hⁿ_δ(A) = ∞) gives Lⁿ(A) ≤ Hⁿ_δ(A).

B.2 (Lⁿ-null sets are Hⁿ_δ-null; “by Definitions 2.2, 2.7”.) Let Lⁿ(Z) = 0 and η > 0. By (2.7) Z ⊆ ⋃_k I_k with open boxes I_k and Σ_k |I_k| < η. A box with side lengths ℓ_1, …, ℓ_n is covered by the closed grid cubes of side s meeting it, whose total volume is ≤ ∏_i(ℓ_i + 2s) → |I| as s ↓ 0; choose s = s_k so small that this total is ≤ |I_k| + 2^{−k}η and s_k√n < δ. This gives countably many closed cubes Q of diameter s√n < δ covering Z with Σ Lⁿ(Q) ≤ 2η, so Hⁿ_δ(Z) ≤ Σ ω_n (s√n/2)ⁿ = ω_n (√n/2)ⁿ Σ Lⁿ(Q) ≤ 2ω_n(√n/2)ⁿ η. As η is arbitrary, Hⁿ_δ(Z) = 0.

B.3 (printed packing lemma) For every bounded open U ⊆ ℝⁿ there are pairwise disjoint closed balls B_1, B_2, … ⊆ U with diam B_j < δ and Lⁿ(U ∖ ⋃_j B_j) = 0.
 Let θ_n := ω_n/4ⁿ ∈ (0, 1). Claim: every nonempty bounded open W contains finitely many pairwise disjoint closed balls of diameter < δ with Lⁿ(W ∖ ⋃ balls) ≤ (1 − θ_n/2) Lⁿ(W). Indeed, write W = ⋃_j Q_j with countably many closed dyadic cubes Q_j with pairwise disjoint interiors and diam Q_j < δ; in Q_j (edge ℓ_j) take the closed ball B'_j concentric with Q_j of radius ℓ_j/3, so B'_j ⊆ int Q_j, diam B'_j < diam Q_j < δ, the B'_j are pairwise disjoint, and Lⁿ(B'_j) = ω_n 3^{−n} ℓ_jⁿ ≥ θ_n Lⁿ(Q_j). As cube boundaries are null, Lⁿ(W ∖ ⋃_j B'_j) = Σ_j Lⁿ(Q_j ∖ B'_j) ≤ (1 − θ_n) Σ_j Lⁿ(Q_j) = (1 − θ_n)Lⁿ(W). Since 0 < Lⁿ(W) < ∞ and Lⁿ(W ∖ ⋃_{j≤N} B'_j) ↓ Lⁿ(W ∖ ⋃_j B'_j), some N gives Lⁿ(W ∖ ⋃_{j≤N} B'_j) ≤ (1 − θ_n/2)Lⁿ(W).
 Now set W_0 := U and, while W_m ≠ ∅, apply the claim to W_m and let W_{m+1} := W_m ∖ (the chosen finitely many balls), which is open and bounded. The balls chosen at all stages are countably many, pairwise disjoint (each stage's balls lie in W_m, which is disjoint from all earlier balls), contained in U, of diameter < δ, and U ∖ ⋃(all balls) ⊆ W_m with Lⁿ(W_m) ≤ (1 − θ_n/2)^m Lⁿ(U) → 0.

B.4 (printed (1)–(3)) Hⁿ_δ(A) ≤ Lⁿ(A). Let {I_k} be any countable cover of A by open boxes. For each k let {B_{kj}}_j be balls as in B.3 for U = I_k, with radii ρ_{kj} (so diam B_{kj} = 2ρ_{kj} < δ). Using the subadditivity of Hⁿ_δ, B.2, and the one-set covers {B_{kj}}:
  Hⁿ_δ(I_k) ≤ Hⁿ_δ(⋃_j B_{kj}) + Hⁿ_δ(I_k ∖ ⋃_j B_{kj}) ≤ Σ_j ω_n ρ_{kj}ⁿ + 0 = Σ_j Lⁿ(B_{kj}) = Lⁿ(⋃_j B_{kj}) ≤ Lⁿ(I_k) = |I_k|.
Hence Hⁿ_δ(A) ≤ Σ_k Hⁿ_δ(I_k) ≤ Σ_k |I_k|, and taking the infimum over box covers (2.7) gives Hⁿ_δ(A) ≤ Lⁿ(A).

B.5 Conclusion of (2.9). By B.1 and B.4, Hⁿ_δ(A) = Lⁿ(A) for every real δ > 0. Hence Hⁿ(A) = sup_{real δ>0} Hⁿ_δ(A) = Lⁿ(A) (the value δ = ∞ in Lean's supremum over δ ∈ (0, ∞] does not change it, since Hⁿ_∞(A) ≤ Hⁿ_1(A) = Lⁿ(A)). Therefore Lⁿ(A) = Hⁿ(A) = Hⁿ_δ(A) for every real δ > 0, which is `LebesgueEqHausdorff`; together with Part A (and Part 0) this proves the conjunction. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.simon_theorem_2_9 n (hδ : 0 < ENNReal.ofReal δ) A` gives `volume A = simonHausdorffOuterValue n A ∧ simonHausdorffOuterValue n A = simonHausdorffContent n (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A`, where `simonHausdorffOuterValue m A` is by definition `simonHausdorffOuterMeasureReal m A`; `simon_theorem_2_10 n A` gives the isodiametric inequality with the real power `(n : ℝ)`, converted by `ENNReal.rpow_natCast` (both in Chapter01/EuclideanNormalization.lean).
proof_key_steps: n = 0: L⁰ and every H⁰_δ are the unit point mass on ℝ⁰, so both statements hold.
Isodiametric inequality: reduce to nonempty compact A and use Steiner symmetrization S_j.
S_j(A) is compact (upper semicontinuity of slice length), has the same measure (Fubini), no larger diameter, and preserves the reflection symmetries already present.
Ã = S_n ⋯ S_1(A) is symmetric under x ↦ −x, so Ã ⊆ B_{diam Ã/2}(0) and Lⁿ(A) ≤ ω_n(diam A/2)ⁿ.
Lⁿ(A) ≤ Hⁿ_δ(A) by subadditivity and the isodiametric inequality on each covering set.
Hⁿ_δ(A) ≤ Lⁿ(A): Lⁿ-null sets are Hⁿ_δ-null, and each open box is packed up to a null set by disjoint closed balls of diameter < δ.
Hence Lⁿ = Hⁿ_δ for every real δ > 0, and Lⁿ = Hⁿ (the δ = ∞ term of the supremum is harmless).

subproblems.title: Upper density comparison and upper density theorem (Simon 3.3, 3.6, with 3.4, 3.5)
subproblems.statement: For metric spaces X (in a common universe) and Borel regular outer measures μ on X, and real n ≥ 0: (3.3) if t ≥ 0 is real, A₁ ⊆ A₂ ⊆ X and Θ^{*n}(μ, A₂, x) ≥ t for all x ∈ A₁, then t·Hⁿ(A₁) ≤ μ(A₂); (3.6) if A ⊆ X is μ-measurable with μ(A) < ∞, then Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) = 0 for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ X ∖ A.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `UpperDensityComparison.{u} ∧ UpperDensityTheorem.{u}` (Simon, Ch. 1, Lemma 3.4, Corollary 3.5, Theorems 3.3 and 3.6; printed proofs, transcribed and completed).

Statements. Let (X, d) be a metric space and μ a Borel regular outer measure on X; n ≥ 0 real.
 (3.3) If t ≥ 0, A₁ ⊆ A₂ ⊆ X (not necessarily measurable) and Θ^{*n}(μ, A₂, x) ≥ t for all x ∈ A₁, then t·Hⁿ(A₁) ≤ μ(A₂).
 (3.6) If A ⊆ X is μ-measurable with μ(A) < ∞, then Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) = 0 for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ X ∖ A, i.e. Hⁿ({x ∉ A : Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) ≠ 0}) = 0.

Conventions. B_ρ(x) is the closed ball. Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) := limsup_{ρ↓0} μ(A ∩ B_ρ(x))/(ω_n ρⁿ) ∈ [0, ∞] (3.1), where ω_n = π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2+1) ∈ (0, ∞) and ω_n ρⁿ ∈ (0, ∞) for ρ > 0 (= 1 when n = 0). Hⁿ_δ and Hⁿ = sup_{δ>0} Hⁿ_δ = lim_{δ↓0} Hⁿ_δ as in (2.1), (2.2) (empty covering sets cost 0; a cover set C costs ω_n(diam C/2)ⁿ, a non-decreasing function of diam C). In [0, ∞], 0·∞ = 0. A “ball” in a family is a pair (x, ρ) with ρ > 0, denoting the closed ball B_ρ(x); B̂ := B_{5ρ}(x). Closed balls are Borel, hence μ-measurable; μ is countably additive on μ-measurable sets (Remark 1.7) and μ(S ∩ ⋃_j E_j) = Σ_j μ(S ∩ E_j) for pairwise disjoint μ-measurable E_j and any S.

Dependency. Theorem 1.15 = sibling `borel_regular_approximation`.

PART I: Theorem 3.3.

I.1 (5-times covering lemma 3.4, in radius form). Let 𝓑 be a family of balls with R := sup{ρ : (x, ρ) ∈ 𝓑} < ∞. There is a subfamily 𝓑' ⊆ 𝓑 of pairwise disjoint closed balls such that
 (*) for every (x, ρ) ∈ 𝓑 there is (x', ρ') ∈ 𝓑' with B_ρ(x) ∩ B_{ρ'}(x') ≠ ∅ and ρ' ≥ ρ/2; consequently B_ρ(x) ⊆ B_{5ρ'}(x').
Proof (printed, with radii in place of diameters so that no ball is lost when a closed ball has diameter 0). For j ≥ 1 let 𝓑_j := {(x, ρ) ∈ 𝓑 : R/2^j < ρ ≤ R/2^{j−1}}; since all ρ > 0, 𝓑 is the disjoint union of the 𝓑_j. Let 𝓑'_1 be a maximal pairwise disjoint subfamily of 𝓑_1, and for j ≥ 2 a maximal pairwise disjoint subfamily 𝓑'_j of {B ∈ 𝓑_j : B ∩ B' = ∅ for all B' ∈ 𝓑'_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝓑'_{j−1}}; these exist by Zorn's lemma (pairwise disjoint subfamilies, ordered by inclusion; the union of a chain is again pairwise disjoint). 𝓑' := ⋃_j 𝓑'_j is pairwise disjoint. If B = (x, ρ) ∈ 𝓑_j, then B meets some B' = (x', ρ') ∈ 𝓑'_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝓑'_j (otherwise 𝓑'_j ∪ {B} would contradict the maximality of 𝓑'_j; if B ∈ 𝓑'_j take B' = B), and B' ∈ 𝓑'_i with i ≤ j gives ρ' > R/2^i ≥ R/2^j ≥ ρ/2. For y ∈ B_ρ(x) and z ∈ B_ρ(x) ∩ B_{ρ'}(x'): d(y, x') ≤ d(y, x) + d(x, z) + d(z, x') ≤ 2ρ + ρ' ≤ 5ρ'.

I.2 (Corollary 3.5.) Suppose moreover that every ball of 𝓑 is centred in a set A₁ and that 𝓑 covers A₁ finely: for every x ∈ A₁ and ε > 0 there is ρ ∈ (0, ε) with (x, ρ) ∈ 𝓑. Then for every finite F ⊆ 𝓑',
  A₁ ∖ ⋃_{B∈F} B ⊆ ⋃_{B'∈𝓑'∖F} B̂'.
Proof. Let x ∈ A₁ ∖ ⋃_{B∈F} B. The finite union of closed balls is closed, so some open ball U_ε(x) misses it; choose (x, ρ) ∈ 𝓑 with ρ < ε, so B_ρ(x) ⊆ U_ε(x) is disjoint from every B ∈ F. By (*) some B' ∈ 𝓑' meets B_ρ(x) and B_ρ(x) ⊆ B̂'; B' ∉ F because it meets B_ρ(x); and x ∈ B_ρ(x) ⊆ B̂'.

I.3 Proof of 3.3. If t = 0 the claim reads 0 ≤ μ(A₂); if μ(A₂) = ∞ it is trivial. So assume t > 0 and μ(A₂) < ∞. Fix τ ∈ (0, t) and δ > 0. For x ∈ A₁ we have Θ^{*n}(μ, A₂, x) ≥ t > τ, so for every ε > 0 there is ρ ∈ (0, ε) with μ(A₂ ∩ B_ρ(x)) > τ ω_n ρⁿ (a limsup exceeding τ is exceeded by values at arbitrarily small ρ). Let
  𝓑 := {(x, ρ) : x ∈ A₁, 0 < ρ < δ/2, μ(A₂ ∩ B_ρ(x)) ≥ τ ω_n ρⁿ}.
Then R ≤ δ/2 and 𝓑 covers A₁ finely; let 𝓑' be as in I.1.
 • 𝓑' is countable: for distinct B_1, …, B_N ∈ 𝓑' (pairwise disjoint, μ-measurable), Σ_{i≤N} μ(A₂ ∩ B_i) = μ(A₂ ∩ ⋃_i B_i) ≤ μ(A₂), and each term is ≥ τω_n ρ_iⁿ > 0; hence for each m at most m·μ(A₂) members of 𝓑' satisfy μ(A₂ ∩ B) > 1/m, and every member satisfies this for some m.
 • If 𝓑' = ∅ then 𝓑 = ∅ by (*), hence A₁ = ∅ by fineness, and the claim is trivial. Otherwise enumerate 𝓑' = {B_{ρ_j}(x_j) : j ∈ J}, J = {1, …, N₀} or J = ℕ_{≥1}. By countable additivity,
   Σ_j ω_n ρ_jⁿ ≤ τ^{−1} Σ_j μ(A₂ ∩ B_{ρ_j}(x_j)) = τ^{−1} μ(A₂ ∩ ⋃_j B_{ρ_j}(x_j)) ≤ τ^{−1} μ(A₂) < ∞.
 • For every N (N ≤ N₀ if J is finite), I.2 with F = {B_{ρ_1}(x_1), …, B_{ρ_N}(x_N)} gives
   A₁ ⊆ ⋃_{j≤N} B_{ρ_j}(x_j) ∪ ⋃_{j>N} B_{5ρ_j}(x_j).
  Each B_{ρ_j}(x_j) has diameter ≤ 2ρ_j < δ < 5δ and each B_{5ρ_j}(x_j) has diameter ≤ 10ρ_j < 5δ, so by (2.2)
   Hⁿ_{5δ}(A₁) ≤ Σ_{j≤N} ω_n ρ_jⁿ + Σ_{j>N} ω_n (5ρ_j)ⁿ = Σ_{j≤N} ω_n ρ_jⁿ + 5ⁿ Σ_{j>N} ω_n ρ_jⁿ.
  Letting N → ∞ (the tail of a convergent series tends to 0; if J is finite take N = N₀) gives Hⁿ_{5δ}(A₁) ≤ Σ_j ω_n ρ_jⁿ ≤ τ^{−1}μ(A₂).
Letting δ ↓ 0 gives τ·Hⁿ(A₁) ≤ μ(A₂), and letting τ ↑ t gives t·Hⁿ(A₁) ≤ μ(A₂). (Formally: ENNReal.ofReal t · Hⁿ(A₁) ≤ μ(A₂).)

PART II: Theorem 3.6.

II.1 (remarks after (1.12)) Let A be μ-measurable with μ(A) < ∞ and μ_A(S) := μ(A ∩ S). Then μ_A is Borel regular and finite. [μ-measurable sets are μ_A-measurable: μ_A(S) = μ(S∩A∩E) + μ((S∩A)∖E) = μ_A(S∩E) + μ_A(S∖E). Borel hulls: take Borel B₁ ⊇ A with μ(B₁) = μ(A), so μ(B₁ ∖ A) = 0; Borel B₂ ⊇ B₁ ∖ A with μ(B₂) = 0; for S take Borel B₃ ⊇ S ∩ A with μ(B₃) = μ(S ∩ A); then B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ B₁) ∪ B₂ is Borel, contains S, and μ_A(B) ≤ μ(B₃) + μ(A ∖ B₁) + μ(B₂) = μ_A(S).]

II.2 (locality) If C is closed and x ∉ C then B_ρ(x) ∩ C = ∅ for all small ρ > 0, so for any E ⊆ X, E ∩ B_ρ(x) = (E ∖ C) ∩ B_ρ(x) for small ρ and Θ^{*n}(μ, E, x) = Θ^{*n}(μ, E ∖ C, x).

II.3 Let t > 0, S_t := {x ∈ X ∖ A : Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) ≥ t}, and let C ⊆ A be closed. Then S_t ⊆ X ∖ C, and for x ∈ S_t, by II.2,
  Θ^{*n}(μ_A, X ∖ C, x) = Θ^{*n}(μ, A ∩ (X ∖ C), x) = Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) ≥ t
(since μ_A((X ∖ C) ∩ B_ρ(x)) = μ(A ∩ (X ∖ C) ∩ B_ρ(x))). Applying Part I to the Borel regular μ_A with A₁ := S_t ⊆ A₂ := X ∖ C yields t·Hⁿ(S_t) ≤ μ_A(X ∖ C) = μ(A ∖ C).

II.4 By Theorem 1.15(2) (sibling `borel_regular_approximation`) applied to μ_A — Borel regular (II.1), open σ-finite with V_n := X since μ_A(X) = μ(A) < ∞, and in a metric space every closed set is a countable intersection of open sets (C = ⋂_k {x : dist(x, C) < 1/k} for C ≠ ∅) — and to the μ_A-measurable set A: μ(A) = μ_A(A) = sup{μ_A(C) : C closed ⊆ A} = sup{μ(C) : C closed ⊆ A}. Choose closed C_k ⊆ A with μ(C_k) → μ(A); as C_k is μ-measurable and μ(A) < ∞, μ(A ∖ C_k) = μ(A) − μ(C_k) → 0. By II.3, t·Hⁿ(S_t) ≤ μ(A ∖ C_k) → 0, so Hⁿ(S_t) = 0.

II.5 {x ∉ A : Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) ≠ 0} = ⋃_{i≥1} S_{1/i}, a countable union of Hⁿ-null sets, hence Hⁿ-null. This is exactly the formal statement ∀ᵐ x ∂Hⁿ, x ∉ A → Θ^{*n}(μ, A, x) = 0. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.simon_theorem_3_3` (identical hypotheses and conclusion) and `simon_theorem_3_6` (null-set form Hⁿ{x | x ∉ A ∧ Θ ≠ 0} = 0; convert with `ae_iff` and `not_imp`) in Chapter01/DensityComparison.lean. The frozen statement fixes one universe `u` for both conjuncts; the parent uses `.1` and `.2` separately.
proof_key_steps: 5-times covering lemma in radius form, via Zorn's lemma on dyadic radius classes.
Corollary 3.5: what finitely many selected balls miss is covered by the 5-fold enlargements of the remaining selected balls.
3.3: the balls with μ(A₂ ∩ B_ρ(x)) ≥ τω_nρⁿ, ρ < δ/2, cover A₁ finely; the disjoint subfamily is countable and Σω_nρ_jⁿ ≤ τ^{−1}μ(A₂).
Hⁿ_{5δ}(A₁) ≤ Σ_{j≤N}ω_nρ_jⁿ + 5ⁿΣ_{j>N}ω_nρ_jⁿ → ≤ τ^{−1}μ(A₂); let δ ↓ 0 and τ ↑ t.
3.6: μ⌞A is Borel regular and finite; for closed C ⊆ A, 3.3 with (μ⌞A, S_t, X ∖ C) gives t·Hⁿ(S_t) ≤ μ(A ∖ C).
Theorem 1.15(2) for μ⌞A gives closed C_k ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ C_k) → 0, so Hⁿ(S_t) = 0; take the union over t = 1/i.

subproblems.title: Besicovitch covering lemma (Simon 3.12; proof from Evans–Gariepy)
subproblems.statement: For each n there is N = N(n) such that for every set B of pairs (centre in ℝⁿ, radius > 0) with radii bounded above, there are N subfamilies D_1, …, D_N ⊆ B, each consisting of pairwise disjoint closed balls, whose balls cover the set of centres of B.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `BesicovitchCovering` (Simon, Ch. 1, Lemma 3.12).

The book gives no proof (“For the proof of this lemma we refer for example to [EG92] or [Fed69]”). We supply the proof of the cited source, L. C. Evans and R. F. Gariepy, Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions (1992, §1.5.2, Theorem 2; revised ed. 2015, Theorem 1.27), adapted to the statement below.

Statement. For each n ∈ ℕ there is N = N(n) ∈ ℕ such that: for every set B ⊆ ℝⁿ × ℝ (ℝⁿ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)) of pairs b = (b.1, b.2) (“centre”, “radius”) with b.2 > 0 for all b ∈ B and {b.2 : b ∈ B} bounded above, there are D_1, …, D_N ⊆ B (indexed by Fin N) such that for each j the closed balls B(b) := {y : |y − b.1| ≤ b.2}, b ∈ D_j, are pairwise disjoint (distinct elements of D_j have disjoint balls), and the set of centres A := {b.1 : b ∈ B} satisfies A ⊆ ⋃_j ⋃_{b∈D_j} B(b).

Constants (depending only on n). α_n := Lⁿ(unit ball) > 0 (for n = 0, L⁰ is the unit point mass and α_0 = 1; all volume comparisons below are valid for every n ≥ 0, a ball of radius r having volume α_n rⁿ). c₀ := (3/32)^{1/2}; L_n := ⌊(1 + 2/c₀)ⁿ⌋; M_n := 20ⁿ + L_n; N := 2(M_n + 1). N is chosen before B, as the quantifier order requires.

Trivial case. If B = ∅ take D_j := ∅. Assume B ≠ ∅ and let R := sup{b.2 : b ∈ B} ∈ (0, ∞).

STEP 1 (bounded set of centres). Claim: if A is bounded, there are 𝒢_1, …, 𝒢_{M_n+1} ⊆ B, each with pairwise disjoint balls, such that A ⊆ ⋃_i ⋃_{b∈𝒢_i} B(b).
 1.1 Selection. Choose b_1 = (a_1, r_1) ∈ B with r_1 > (3/4)R. Inductively, for j ≥ 2 let A_j := A ∖ ⋃_{i<j} B(b_i). If A_j = ∅ stop and put J := j − 1; otherwise s_j := sup{r : (a, r) ∈ B, a ∈ A_j} ∈ (0, R] and choose b_j = (a_j, r_j) ∈ B with a_j ∈ A_j and r_j > (3/4)s_j. If the process never stops put J := ∞.
 1.2 For i < j ≤ J: a_j ∈ A_j ⊆ A_i, so r_j ≤ s_i < (4/3)r_i; and a_j ∉ B(b_i), i.e. |a_j − a_i| > r_i. In particular the a_j are distinct, so the b_j are distinct elements of B.
 1.3 The balls B(a_j, r_j/3) are pairwise disjoint: for i < j, r_i/3 + r_j/3 < r_i/3 + 4r_i/9 < r_i < |a_i − a_j|.
 1.4 If J = ∞ then r_j → 0: A ⊆ B_M(0) for some M, so the disjoint balls B(a_j, r_j/3) lie in B_{M+R}(0); if r_j ≥ c > 0 for infinitely many j, infinitely many disjoint balls of volume ≥ α_n(c/3)ⁿ would lie in a set of finite volume.
 1.5 A ⊆ ⋃_{j≤J} B(b_j). If J < ∞ this is A_{J+1} = ∅. If J = ∞ and a ∈ A, pick (a, r) ∈ B; by 1.4 some j has r_j < (3/4)r; if a ∉ ⋃_{i<j} B(b_i) then a ∈ A_j, so s_j ≥ r and r_j > (3/4)r, a contradiction.
 1.6 Fix k ≤ J with k ≥ 2 and let I_k := {j < k : B(b_j) ∩ B(b_k) ≠ ∅}, K₁ := {j ∈ I_k : r_j ≤ 3r_k}, K₂ := {j ∈ I_k : r_j > 3r_k}. We show #I_k ≤ M_n.
 1.7 #K₁ ≤ 20ⁿ. For j ∈ K₁, |a_j − a_k| ≤ r_j + r_k ≤ 4r_k, so B(a_j, r_j/3) ⊆ B(a_k, 5r_k); and j < k gives r_k < (4/3)r_j, i.e. r_j/3 > r_k/4. These balls are disjoint (1.3), so #K₁·α_n(r_k/4)ⁿ ≤ α_n(5r_k)ⁿ, i.e. #K₁ ≤ 20ⁿ.
 1.8 (Angle estimate.) Let i ≠ j in K₂, x := a_i − a_k, y := a_j − a_k. For l ∈ {i, j} (l < k): (a) 3r_k < r_l; (b) r_l < |a_l − a_k| (1.2, as a_k ∉ B(b_l)); (c) |a_l − a_k| ≤ r_l + r_k (the balls meet). In particular x, y ≠ 0. Claim: ⟨x, y⟩ ≤ (61/64)|x||y|. The claim is symmetric in i, j, so we may assume |x| ≤ |y|. Suppose cos θ := ⟨x, y⟩/(|x||y|) > 61/64.
  (α) a_i ∈ B(b_j), i.e. |x − y| ≤ r_j. Otherwise |x − y| > r_j. If |x − y| ≥ |y|, then cos θ = (|x|² + |y|² − |x − y|²)/(2|x||y|) ≤ |x|/(2|y|) ≤ 1/2. If r_j < |x − y| < |y|, then |y|² − |x − y|² ≤ 2|y|(|y| − |x − y|) < 2|y|(|y| − r_j) ≤ 2|y|r_k by (c), so cos θ < |x|/(2|y|) + r_k/|x| ≤ 1/2 + r_k/(3r_k) = 5/6, using |x| > r_i > 3r_k. Either way cos θ ≤ 5/6 < 61/64, a contradiction.
  (β) Hence i < j: if j < i then a_i ∈ A_i is outside B(b_j) by construction, contradicting (α). By 1.2, r_j < (4/3)r_i and |x − y| = |a_j − a_i| > r_i.
  (γ) But 0 ≤ |y| − |x| < (r_j + r_k) − r_i < (4/3)r_i + r_i/3 − r_i = (2/3)r_i and |x||y| ≤ (r_i + r_k)(r_j + r_k) < (4/3)r_i·(5/3)r_i = (20/9)r_i², so
     |x − y|² = (|y| − |x|)² + 2|x||y|(1 − cos θ) < (4/9)r_i² + 2·(20/9)·(3/64)r_i² = (47/72)r_i² < r_i²,
     contradicting (β). Hence cos θ ≤ 61/64.
 1.9 #K₂ ≤ L_n. The unit vectors u_l := (a_l − a_k)/|a_l − a_k| (l ∈ K₂) satisfy |u_i − u_j|² = 2 − 2cos θ ≥ 2 − 122/64 = 3/32 for i ≠ j, i.e. |u_i − u_j| ≥ c₀. The open balls of radius c₀/2 about the u_l are pairwise disjoint and contained in the ball of radius 1 + c₀/2 about 0, so #K₂·α_n(c₀/2)ⁿ ≤ α_n(1 + c₀/2)ⁿ, i.e. #K₂ ≤ (1 + 2/c₀)ⁿ, hence #K₂ ≤ L_n. (For n = 0 there are no unit vectors and K₂ = ∅.)
 1.10 So #I_k ≤ 20ⁿ + L_n = M_n for every k. Colouring: put b_1 into 𝒢_1; for k = 2, 3, … (k ≤ J) the ball B(b_k) meets at most M_n of the balls B(b_j), j < k, so some 𝒢_i (1 ≤ i ≤ M_n + 1) contains no b_j (j < k) with B(b_j) ∩ B(b_k) ≠ ∅; put b_k into the first such 𝒢_i. Then each 𝒢_i ⊆ B has pairwise disjoint balls (if b_j, b_k ∈ 𝒢_i with j < k, then B(b_j) ∩ B(b_k) = ∅), and A ⊆ ⋃_{j≤J} B(b_j) = ⋃_i ⋃_{b∈𝒢_i} B(b) by 1.5.

STEP 2 (general case). For m ≥ 1 let B^m := {b ∈ B : 3R(m − 1) ≤ |b.1| < 3Rm}; its set of centres is bounded and the B^m partition B. Step 1 applied to B^m (with R replaced by the supremum R_m ≤ R of the radii occurring in B^m; if B^m = ∅ take empty families) gives 𝒢^m_1, …, 𝒢^m_{M_n+1} ⊆ B^m with pairwise disjoint balls covering the centres of B^m. If b ∈ B^m and b' ∈ B^{m'} with m' ≥ m + 2, then |b'.1| − |b.1| > 3R(m' − 1) − 3Rm ≥ 3R > b.2 + b'.2, so B(b) ∩ B(b') = ∅. For i = 1, …, M_n + 1 put
  D_i := ⋃_{m odd} 𝒢^m_i,   D_{M_n+1+i} := ⋃_{m even} 𝒢^m_i.
Each D_l ⊆ B has pairwise disjoint balls (two members from the same B^m are disjoint by Step 1; members from different B^m, B^{m'} of the same parity have |m − m'| ≥ 2), and ⋃_l ⋃_{b∈D_l} B(b) contains the centres of every B^m, i.e. all of A. Indexing the N = 2(M_n + 1) families by Fin N gives the statement, with N depending only on n. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): Mathlib's `Besicovitch.exist_disjoint_covering_families` (Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Covering/Besicovitch.lean, with `Besicovitch.multiplicity` and `isEmpty_satelliteConfig_multiplicity` from BesicovitchVectorSpace.lean) is the same theorem for an arbitrary index type and open balls; `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.exists_besicovitchCovering_families` (Chapter01/Densities.lean) restates it with closed balls and N = `Besicovitch.multiplicity (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))`. Apply it with index type ↥B, c := (·.1.1), r := (·.1.2), and push each family forward along `Subtype.val` (injective, so disjointness transfers via `Set.InjOn.pairwiseDisjoint_image`).
proof_key_steps: Fix N := 2(20ⁿ + ⌊(1 + 2/c₀)ⁿ⌋ + 1), c₀ = (3/32)^{1/2}, depending only on n.
Bounded centres: greedy selection with r_j > (3/4)·sup of available radii; r_j < (4/3)r_i for i < j; the r_j/3-balls are disjoint; r_j → 0; the selected balls cover the centres.
Each selected ball meets at most 20ⁿ earlier balls of comparable radius (volume count).
Angle lemma: earlier large balls meeting B_k are seen from a_k under pairwise angles with cos ≤ 61/64, so there are at most ⌊(1 + 2/c₀)ⁿ⌋ of them.
Greedy colouring of the selected balls into M_n + 1 disjoint families.
General case: annuli of width 3R; odd and even annuli give 2(M_n + 1) disjoint families covering all centres.

subproblems.title: General density theorem and Lebesgue differentiation (Simon 3.16, 3.17, with 3.11(1), 3.13, 3.15)
subproblems.statement: For metric spaces X (in a common universe) and outer measures μ on X that are Borel regular, open σ-finite and have the Symmetric Vitali Property: (3.16) for every μ-measurable A, μ(A ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) → 1 as ρ ↓ 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ A and → 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ X ∖ A; (3.17) for every μ-measurable f : X → ℝ such that each x has some ρ > 0 with ∫_{B_ρ(x)} |f| dμ < ∞, μ(B_ρ(x))^{−1}∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ → f(x) as ρ ↓ 0 for μ-a.e. x.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `GeneralDensityTheorem.{u} ∧ LebesgueDifferentiation.{u}` (Simon, Ch. 1, Remark 3.11(1), Theorems 3.13, 3.15, 3.16 and Corollary 3.17; printed proofs, transcribed and completed).

Statements. Let (X, d) be a metric space and μ an outer measure on X which is Borel regular, open σ-finite (X = ⋃_j V_j, V_j open, μ(V_j) < ∞) and has the Symmetric Vitali Property (SVP; Def. 3.10 as formalized: for every A ⊆ X with μ(A) < ∞ and every set 𝓑 of pairs (x, r) with x ∈ A, r > 0, which is fine on A — for all x ∈ A and ε > 0 there is r ∈ (0, ε) with (x, r) ∈ 𝓑 — there is a countable 𝓑' ⊆ 𝓑 whose closed balls B_r(x) are pairwise disjoint and μ(A ∖ ⋃_{(x,r)∈𝓑'} B_r(x)) = 0).
 (3.16) If A is μ-measurable, then q_x(ρ) := μ(A ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) → 1 as ρ ↓ 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ A, and q_x(ρ) → 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ X ∖ A.
 (3.17) If f : X → ℝ is μ-measurable and every x has some ρ_x > 0 with ∫_{B_{ρ_x}(x)} |f| dμ < ∞, then for μ-a.e. x, (μ(B_ρ(x)))^{−1} ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ → f(x) as ρ ↓ 0.

Conventions. Quotients of values in [0, ∞] use the conventions of [0, ∞]: a/0 = ∞ for a > 0, 0/0 = 0, a/∞ = 0 for a < ∞ (Lean `ENNReal`); at all points that matter below the denominators are in (0, ∞). Integrals are with respect to μ on the σ-algebra M_μ of μ-measurable sets (Lemma 1.6/Remark 1.7; Lean `caratheodoryMeasure μ`); “μ-measurable function” means M_μ-measurable. “P for μ-a.e. x ∈ E” means μ({x ∈ E : not P(x)}) = 0. In the formal statement of 3.17 the average is written (μ(B_ρ(x))).toReal⁻¹ · ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ (Bochner integral); at the points and radii used below 0 < μ(B_ρ(x)) < ∞ and f is integrable on B_ρ(x), so this is the usual average. Standard facts: M_μ is a σ-algebra containing all μ-null sets, μ is countably additive on it; a countable union of null sets is null.

Dependency. Theorem 1.15 = sibling `borel_regular_approximation` (used for finite Borel regular measures; in a metric space every closed set C ≠ ∅ equals ⋂_k {dist(·, C) < 1/k}, a countable intersection of open sets).

STEP 1 (restriction lemma; remarks after (1.12)). Let σ be a Borel regular outer measure and Y ⊆ X either Borel, or σ-measurable with σ(Y) < ∞. Then σ⌞Y (S ↦ σ(Y ∩ S)) is Borel regular, and every σ-measurable set is σ⌞Y-measurable.
 Proof. For E σ-measurable: σ⌞Y(S) = σ(S∩Y∩E) + σ((S∩Y)∖E) = σ⌞Y(S∩E) + σ⌞Y(S∖E); so Borel sets are σ⌞Y-measurable. Borel hulls, Y Borel: for S take Borel B₃ ⊇ S ∩ Y with σ(B₃) = σ(S ∩ Y); B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ Y) is Borel, contains S, and σ⌞Y(B) ≤ σ(B₃) = σ⌞Y(S). Y measurable with σ(Y) < ∞: take Borel B₁ ⊇ Y with σ(B₁) = σ(Y), so σ(B₁ ∖ Y) = 0, and Borel B₂ ⊇ B₁ ∖ Y with σ(B₂) = 0; then B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ B₁) ∪ B₂ ⊇ S is Borel and σ⌞Y(B) ≤ σ(B₃) + σ(Y ∖ B₁) + σ(B₂) = σ⌞Y(S).

STEP 2 (localization to finite measures). For each j let μ_j := μ⌞V_j. Then μ_j is Borel regular (Step 1, V_j open), finite (μ_j(X) = μ(V_j) < ∞), and has the SVP: if μ_j(A) = μ(A ∩ V_j) < ∞ and 𝓑 is fine on A, then the pairs of 𝓑 centred in A ∩ V_j form a family fine on A ∩ V_j, and the SVP of μ yields a countable disjoint 𝓑' with μ((A ∩ V_j) ∖ ⋃𝓑') = 0, i.e. μ_j(A ∖ ⋃𝓑') = 0. Every μ-measurable set is μ_j-measurable (Step 1). For x ∈ V_j there is ρ_x' > 0 with B_ρ(x) ⊆ V_j for ρ < ρ_x' (V_j open), and then μ_j(E ∩ B_ρ(x)) = μ(E ∩ B_ρ(x)) for every E ⊆ X. A set N ⊆ V_j is μ-null iff it is μ_j-null. Hence, if a pointwise property of x is determined by the values μ(E ∩ B_ρ(x)) (finitely many fixed E) for arbitrarily small ρ, and it holds μ_j-a.e. for μ_j, then it holds for μ-a.e. x ∈ V_j; as X = ⋃_j V_j, it then holds μ-a.e. on X.

In Steps 3–6, μ and ν denote Borel regular outer measures with μ(X), ν(X) < ∞, μ has the SVP, and U₀ := {x : μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ > 0}.

STEP 3 (Remark 3.11(1)). μ(U₀) = 0. The family {(x, ρ) : x ∈ U₀, ρ > 0, μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0} is fine on U₀ (if μ(B_R(x)) = 0 then μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for all ρ ≤ R). By the SVP (μ(U₀) < ∞) there is a countable disjoint subfamily 𝓑' with μ(U₀ ∖ ⋃𝓑') = 0, and μ(⋃𝓑') ≤ Σ_{𝓑'} μ(B) = 0. Hence μ(U₀) = 0. For x ∉ U₀: 0 < μ(B_ρ(x)) < ∞ for every ρ > 0.

STEP 4 (Theorem 3.13, comparison, finite case). Let A ⊆ X and t > 0 with limsup_{ρ↓0} ν(B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) ≥ t for every x ∈ A ∖ U₀. Then ν(A) ≥ t·μ(A).
 Proof (printed). μ(A) = μ(A ∖ U₀) by Step 3. Let τ ∈ (0, t) and U ⊇ A open. Let 𝓑 := {(x, ρ) : x ∈ A ∖ U₀, ρ > 0, B_ρ(x) ⊆ U, ν(B_ρ(x)) > τ μ(B_ρ(x))}. 𝓑 is fine on A ∖ U₀: for such x the quotient exceeds τ for arbitrarily small ρ (its limsup is ≥ t > τ), B_ρ(x) ⊆ U for small ρ, and as μ(B_ρ(x)) ∈ (0, ∞) the quotient exceeds τ iff ν(B_ρ(x)) > τμ(B_ρ(x)). By the SVP (μ(A ∖ U₀) < ∞) there are countably many disjoint B_j ∈ 𝓑 with μ((A ∖ U₀) ∖ ⋃_j B_j) = 0. Closed balls are ν-measurable, so
  τμ(A) = τμ(A ∖ U₀) ≤ τ Σ_j μ(B_j) ≤ Σ_j ν(B_j) = ν(⋃_j B_j) ≤ ν(U).
 By Theorem 1.15(1) (sibling) for ν (Borel regular, finite, hence open σ-finite with V_n = X), inf_{U⊇A open} ν(U) = ν(A); so τμ(A) ≤ ν(A), and τ ↑ t gives the claim.

STEP 5 (Theorem 3.15, general upper density theorem, finite case; “the proof is essentially the same as the proof of 3.6 with 3.13 in place of 3.3”, details supplied). Let E ⊆ X be ν-measurable. Then for μ-a.e. x ∈ X ∖ E: ν(E ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) → 0 as ρ ↓ 0.
 Proof. For t > 0 let S_t := {x ∈ X ∖ (E ∪ U₀) : limsup_{ρ↓0} ν(E ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) ≥ t}. Let C ⊆ E be closed and ν_C := ν⌞(E ∖ C), Borel regular and finite by Step 1 (E ∖ C is ν-measurable). For x ∈ S_t we have x ∉ C, so B_ρ(x) ∩ C = ∅ for small ρ and ν_C(B_ρ(x)) = ν((E ∖ C) ∩ B_ρ(x)) = ν(E ∩ B_ρ(x)); hence limsup ν_C(B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) ≥ t on S_t = S_t ∖ U₀. Step 4 with ν_C in place of ν gives t·μ(S_t) ≤ ν_C(S_t) ≤ ν(E ∖ C). By Theorem 1.15(2) (sibling) for ν⌞E (Borel regular, finite; E is ν⌞E-measurable) there are closed C_k ⊆ E with ν(C_k) → ν(E), so ν(E ∖ C_k) = ν(E) − ν(C_k) → 0. Thus μ(S_t) = 0. For x ∈ X ∖ (E ∪ U₀ ∪ ⋃_m S_{1/m}) the limsup is 0, so the nonnegative quotient tends to 0; the excluded set is μ-null (Step 3).

STEP 6 (Theorem 3.16, finite case). Let A be μ-measurable. For x ∉ U₀ and ρ > 0, since 0 < μ(B_ρ(x)) < ∞ and A is μ-measurable,
  μ(A ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ(B_ρ(x)) + μ(B_ρ(x) ∖ A)/μ(B_ρ(x)) = 1.
By Step 5 with ν := μ and E := A, the first term → 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ X ∖ A. By Step 5 with ν := μ and E := X ∖ A, the second term → 0, hence the first → 1, for μ-a.e. x ∈ A.

STEP 7 (Theorem 3.16, general; printed “we can assume without loss of generality that μ(X) < ∞”). Let A be μ-measurable. For each j, A is μ_j-measurable and Step 6 for μ_j gives: for μ_j-a.e. x, μ_j(A ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ_j(B_ρ(x)) tends to 1 if x ∈ A and to 0 if x ∉ A. For x ∈ V_j this quotient equals q_x(ρ) for ρ < ρ_x' (Step 2). Hence q_x(ρ) → 1 for μ-a.e. x ∈ A ∩ V_j and q_x(ρ) → 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ V_j ∖ A; taking the union over j proves both clauses of `GeneralDensityTheorem`.

STEP 8 (Borel envelopes, finite case). If σ is Borel regular with σ(X) < ∞ and E is σ-measurable, there is a Borel F ⊇ E with σ(F ∖ E) = 0 (a Borel hull F with σ(F) = σ(E), then σ(F ∖ E) = σ(F) − σ(E) = 0).

STEP 9 (Corollary 3.17 for nonnegative integrable f, finite μ). Assume (as in Steps 3–6) μ finite with the SVP and let f : X → [0, ∞) be μ-measurable with ∫_X f dμ < ∞. Then for μ-a.e. x, avg_ρ(x) := μ(B_ρ(x))^{−1}∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ → f(x).
 9.1 (printed: “let ν₀(A) = ∫_A f dμ for each Borel set A and let ν be the associated Borel regular outer measure as in Remark 1.11”). Put ν(S) := inf{∫_F f dμ : F ⊇ S Borel}. By Remark 1.11, ν is a Borel regular outer measure with ν(F) = ∫_F f dμ for Borel F, and ν(X) = ∫ f dμ < ∞. [Proof of Remark 1.11 here: countable subadditivity follows from countable additivity of F ↦ ∫_F f dμ applied to Borel covers; the infimum is attained (intersect a minimizing sequence of Borel sets); a Borel G is ν-measurable: for S with ν(S) < ∞ choose Borel C ⊇ S with ν(C) = ν(S), then ν(S ∩ G) + ν(S ∖ G) ≤ ∫_{C∩G} f dμ + ∫_{C∖G} f dμ = ∫_C f dμ = ν(S).]
 9.2 Every μ-null set N is ν-null (a Borel G ⊇ N with μ(G) = 0 gives ν(N) ≤ ∫_G f dμ = 0). For μ-measurable E: by Step 8 there is a Borel F ⊇ E with μ(F ∖ E) = 0, so ∫_F f dμ = ∫_E f dμ, while every Borel F' ⊇ E has ∫_{F'} f dμ ≥ ∫_E f dμ; hence ν(E) = ∫_E f dμ. Moreover E = F ∖ (F ∖ E) with F Borel and F ∖ E ν-null, so E is ν-measurable.
 9.3 (printed (*)) For i, j ≥ 1 let A_ij := {x : (j−1)/i ≤ f(x) < j/i} (μ-measurable); for each i, X is the disjoint union of the A_ij, j ≥ 1. For x ∉ U₀, ρ > 0 and B := B_ρ(x), using 9.2:
  ((j−1)/i)·μ(B ∩ A_ij) ≤ ∫_{B∩A_ij} f dμ ≤ ∫_B f dμ = ν(B ∩ A_ij) + ν(B ∖ A_ij) ≤ (j/i)·μ(B ∩ A_ij) + ν(B ∖ A_ij).
 By Step 6, μ(B_ρ(x) ∩ A_ij)/μ(B_ρ(x)) → 1 for μ-a.e. x ∈ A_ij. By Step 5 applied to the pair (ν, μ) (ν finite Borel regular by 9.1) and the ν-measurable set E := X ∖ A_ij (9.2), ν(B_ρ(x) ∖ A_ij)/μ(B_ρ(x)) → 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ A_ij. Dividing by μ(B_ρ(x)) ∈ (0, ∞): for μ-a.e. x ∈ A_ij,
  (j−1)/i ≤ liminf_{ρ↓0} avg_ρ(x) ≤ limsup_{ρ↓0} avg_ρ(x) ≤ j/i,
 and since (j−1)/i ≤ f(x) < j/i on A_ij, f(x) − 1/i ≤ liminf avg ≤ limsup avg ≤ f(x) + 1/i. Removing the countably many exceptional null sets (all i, j, and U₀), for μ-a.e. x this holds for every i, so avg_ρ(x) → f(x).

STEP 10 (integrable signed f, finite μ; printed “since f = max{f,0} − max{−f,0} we can assume f ≥ 0”). If f is μ-measurable with ∫|f| dμ < ∞, apply Step 9 to f⁺ := max{f, 0} and f⁻ := max{−f, 0}; averages are linear, so avg_ρ(f)(x) = avg_ρ(f⁺)(x) − avg_ρ(f⁻)(x) → f⁺(x) − f⁻(x) = f(x) for μ-a.e. x (finite limits).

STEP 11 (localization for the general μ; supplies the reduction “we can assume μ(X) < ∞” when f is only locally integrable). Let f be as in (3.17). Fix j and let 𝓑_j := {(c, r) : c ∈ V_j, r > 0, B_{2r}(c) ⊆ V_j, ∫_{B_{2r}(c)} |f| dμ < ∞}. It is fine on V_j: for c ∈ V_j and ε > 0 choose r < ε with 2r ≤ ρ_c and B_{2r}(c) ⊆ V_j. By the SVP of μ (μ(V_j) < ∞) there is a countable disjoint 𝓓_j ⊆ 𝓑_j with μ(V_j ∖ ⋃_{(c,r)∈𝓓_j} B_r(c)) = 0. For b = (c, r) ∈ 𝓓_j let f_b := f·1_{B_{2r}(c)}; it is μ_j-measurable (μ-measurable sets are μ_j-measurable, Step 1), and since μ_j and μ agree on μ-measurable subsets of V_j, ∫_E g dμ_j = ∫_E g dμ for every μ-measurable g and every μ-measurable E ⊆ V_j (whenever either side is defined); in particular ∫|f_b| dμ_j = ∫_{B_{2r}(c)} |f| dμ < ∞. Step 10 for the finite measure μ_j (Borel regular with the SVP, Step 2) and f_b gives: for μ_j-a.e. x, μ_j(B_ρ(x))^{−1}∫_{B_ρ(x)} f_b dμ_j → f_b(x). If x lies in the open ball U_{2r}(c) and ρ < 2r − d(x, c), then B_ρ(x) ⊆ B_{2r}(c) ⊆ V_j, so μ_j(B_ρ(x)) = μ(B_ρ(x)), ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f_b dμ_j = ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ and f_b(x) = f(x). Hence avg_ρ(x) → f(x) for μ-a.e. x ∈ U_{2r}(c) ⊇ B_r(c). Taking the union over the countably many j and b ∈ 𝓓_j, the convergence holds for μ-a.e. x ∈ ⋃_j ⋃_{(c,r)∈𝓓_j} B_r(c), which contains μ-almost every point of X (each V_j ∖ ⋃_{𝓓_j} B_r(c) is null and ⋃_j V_j = X).

STEP 12 (formal conclusion of 3.17). U₀(μ) := {x : μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ > 0} is μ-null: U₀(μ) ∩ V_j ⊆ U₀(μ_j) and μ(U₀(μ) ∩ V_j) = μ_j(U₀(μ) ∩ V_j) ≤ μ_j(U₀(μ_j)) = 0 by Step 3. For x ∉ U₀(μ), x ∈ V_j, and 0 < ρ < min(ρ_x', ρ_x): 0 < μ(B_ρ(x)) < ∞, so (μ(B_ρ(x))).toReal⁻¹ = 1/μ(B_ρ(x)), and f is integrable on B_ρ(x), so ∫_{B_ρ(x)} f dμ is the Lebesgue integral. Thus the expression in `LebesgueDifferentiation` equals avg_ρ(x) for all small ρ, and Step 11 proves it tends to f(x) for μ-a.e. x. (The formal hypotheses “Measurable[μ.caratheodory] f” and “∫⁻_{B_ρ(x)} ofReal|f| d(caratheodoryMeasure μ) < ∞” are exactly μ-measurability of f and ∫_{B_ρ(x)} |f| dμ < ∞.) Together with Step 7 this proves the conjunction. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.simon_theorem_3_16` (Chapter01/GeneralDensity.lean: a.e. with respect to `hμ.toBorelMeasure`, limit `A.indicator 1 x`; null sets agree with μ's by `toBorelMeasure_apply_all`) and `simon_corollary_3_17_of_caratheodory` (Chapter01/GeneralDifferentiation.lean: same hypotheses, integrals against `hμ.toBorelMeasure`). To transport integrals: `(caratheodoryMeasure μ).trim hμ.borel_le_caratheodory = hμ.toBorelMeasure` (both agree on Borel sets), `f` is a.e. Borel by `IsBorelRegularOuterMeasure.aemeasurable_of_caratheodory`, then `setLIntegral_trim_ae`, `restrict_trim`, `integral_trim_ae`. The frozen statement fixes one universe `u` for both conjuncts.
proof_key_steps: Restriction lemma and localization to the finite measures μ⌞V_j, which remain Borel regular with the Symmetric Vitali Property.
Remark 3.11(1): the zero-ball set U₀ is μ-null, by the Symmetric Vitali Property.
Theorem 3.13 (finite case): an upper density ≥ t on A gives ν(A) ≥ t·μ(A), via the Vitali property and outer regularity (Theorem 1.15(1)).
Theorem 3.15 (finite case): the density of ν⌞E with respect to μ vanishes μ-a.e. off E, via 3.13 and closed inner approximation (Theorem 1.15(2)).
Theorem 3.16: the two complementary quotients sum to 1; apply 3.15 to A and to X ∖ A, then transfer from μ⌞V_j to μ.
Corollary 3.17 for integrable f ≥ 0 and finite μ: ν = f dμ (Remark 1.11); level sets A_ij, 3.16 and 3.15 squeeze the averages within 1/i of f(x).
Signed and locally integrable f: split f = f⁺ − f⁻, and localize by a Vitali-selected countable family of balls on whose doubles f is integrable.
Formal conventions: for μ-a.e. x and small ρ, 0 < μ(B_ρ(x)) < ∞ and f is integrable on B_ρ(x), so toReal⁻¹·∫ is the average.

subproblems.title: Radon–Nikodym theorem via densities (Simon 3.24, with 3.13–3.15, 3.19, 3.21, 3.23)
subproblems.statement: For a metric space X and outer measures μ, μ₀ on X that are Borel regular and open σ-finite, μ₀ with the Symmetric Vitali Property, and Θ(x) := limsup_{ρ↓0} μ(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)): (0) for μ₀-a.e. x the quotient converges to Θ(x); (i) if μ₀(E) = 0 ⇒ μ(E) = 0 for all E, then μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ for every Borel A; (ii) there is a Borel Z with μ₀(Z) = 0 and μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z ∩ A) for every Borel A; (iii) if μ also has the Symmetric Vitali Property, then Z_∞ := {x : the quotient tends to ∞} has μ₀(Z_∞) = 0 and μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z_∞ ∩ A) for every Borel A.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `RadonNikodymTheorem` (Simon, Ch. 1, 3.9–3.24: Remark 3.11(1), Theorems 3.13, 3.14, 3.15, Lemma 3.19, Theorems 3.21, 3.23, 3.24; printed proofs, transcribed and completed).

Statement. Let (X, d) be a metric space, μ, μ₀ Borel regular, open σ-finite outer measures on X, μ₀ with the Symmetric Vitali Property (SVP, Def. 3.10 as formalized: for every A with μ₀(A) < ∞ and every set 𝓑 of pairs (x, r), x ∈ A, r > 0, fine on A — ∀x ∈ A ∀ε > 0 ∃r ∈ (0, ε) with (x, r) ∈ 𝓑 — there is a countable 𝓑' ⊆ 𝓑 with pairwise disjoint closed balls and μ₀(A ∖ ⋃_{𝓑'} B_r(x)) = 0). Write q_x(ρ) := μ(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) ∈ [0, ∞] (B_ρ(x) closed ball; [0, ∞]-conventions a/0 = ∞ for a > 0, 0/0 = 0, a/∞ = 0 for a < ∞), Θ(x) := limsup_{ρ↓0} q_x(ρ) (Lean `outerRelativeUpperDensity μ μ₀ x`; it realizes Simon's three-case definition 3.9), Θ_*(x) := liminf_{ρ↓0} q_x(ρ) (3.18). Integrals ∫_A g dμ₀ are Lebesgue integrals over A for the measure μ₀ on the σ-algebra of μ₀-measurable sets (Lean `caratheodoryMeasure μ₀`). To prove:
 (0) for μ₀-a.e. x, q_x(ρ) → Θ(x) as ρ ↓ 0 (the density Θ^{μ₀}(μ, x) of 3.22 exists and equals Θ(x));
 (i) if μ₀(E) = 0 ⇒ μ(E) = 0 for all E ⊆ X, then μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ for every Borel A;
 (ii) there is a Borel Z with μ₀(Z) = 0 and μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z ∩ A) for every Borel A;
 (iii) if μ also has the SVP, then Z_∞ := {x : q_x(ρ) → ∞ as ρ ↓ 0} has μ₀(Z_∞) = 0 and μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z_∞ ∩ A) for every Borel A.

Standard facts: for an outer measure σ the σ-measurable sets form a σ-algebra M_σ containing all σ-null sets, σ is countably additive on M_σ (Simon 1.6, 1.7); Borel sets are σ-measurable for Borel regular σ; countable unions of null sets are null.

Dependency. Theorem 1.15 = sibling `borel_regular_approximation` (applied to finite Borel regular measures; closed subsets of a metric space are countable intersections of open sets).

PART I. THE FINITE CASE. Throughout Part I assume in addition μ(X) < ∞ and μ₀(X) < ∞. Let U₀ := {x : μ₀(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ > 0}.

I.0 (restriction lemma, remarks after (1.12)). If σ is Borel regular and Y is Borel, or σ-measurable with σ(Y) < ∞, then σ⌞Y (S ↦ σ(Y ∩ S)) is Borel regular and every σ-measurable set is σ⌞Y-measurable. [σ⌞Y(S) = σ(S∩Y∩E) + σ((S∩Y)∖E) for E ∈ M_σ. Hulls: Borel B₃ ⊇ S ∩ Y with σ(B₃) = σ(S ∩ Y); if Y is Borel, B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ Y); otherwise take Borel B₁ ⊇ Y with σ(B₁ ∖ Y) = 0 and Borel B₂ ⊇ B₁ ∖ Y with σ(B₂) = 0 and B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ B₁) ∪ B₂; in both cases B ⊇ S is Borel and σ⌞Y(B) ≤ σ(B₃) = σ⌞Y(S).]

I.1 (Remark 3.11(1)) μ₀(U₀) = 0: the pairs (x, ρ) with x ∈ U₀, μ₀(B_ρ(x)) = 0 form a fine family on U₀; the SVP gives countably many disjoint such balls covering μ₀-almost all of U₀, and their union is μ₀-null. For x ∉ U₀, 0 < μ₀(B_ρ(x)) < ∞ for all ρ > 0. The same argument shows: if a finite Borel regular σ has the SVP then {x : σ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ > 0} is σ-null.

I.2 (Theorem 3.13) Let σ be a Borel regular outer measure with σ(X) < ∞, A ⊆ X, t > 0, and limsup_{ρ↓0} σ(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) ≥ t for all x ∈ A ∖ U₀. Then σ(A) ≥ t·μ₀(A).
 Proof (printed). μ₀(A) = μ₀(A ∖ U₀) (I.1). Let τ ∈ (0, t), U ⊇ A open, and 𝓑 := {(x, ρ) : x ∈ A ∖ U₀, ρ > 0, B_ρ(x) ⊆ U, σ(B_ρ(x)) > τμ₀(B_ρ(x))}; 𝓑 is fine on A ∖ U₀ (the quotient exceeds τ at arbitrarily small ρ, B_ρ(x) ⊆ U for small ρ, μ₀(B_ρ(x)) ∈ (0, ∞)). The SVP of μ₀ gives disjoint B_j ∈ 𝓑 (countably many) with μ₀((A ∖ U₀) ∖ ⋃B_j) = 0, so τμ₀(A) ≤ τΣ_jμ₀(B_j) ≤ Σ_jσ(B_j) = σ(⋃B_j) ≤ σ(U). By Theorem 1.15(1) (sibling) for σ, inf_U σ(U) = σ(A); then let τ ↑ t.

I.3 (Corollary 3.14) μ₀({x : Θ(x) = ∞}) = 0: for t > 0, A_t := {Θ ≥ t} satisfies t·μ₀(A_t) ≤ μ(A_t) ≤ μ(X) by I.2, so μ₀({Θ = ∞}) ≤ μ(X)/t → 0.

I.4 (Theorem 3.15) Let σ be Borel regular with σ(X) < ∞ and E σ-measurable. Then for μ₀-a.e. x ∉ E, σ(E ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) → 0.
 Proof (as in 3.6 with 3.13 in place of 3.3). For t > 0 let S_t := {x ∉ E ∪ U₀ : limsup σ(E ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) ≥ t}. For closed C ⊆ E, σ_C := σ⌞(E ∖ C) is Borel regular and finite (I.0), and for x ∈ S_t (x ∉ C) σ_C(B_ρ(x)) = σ(E ∩ B_ρ(x)) for small ρ; I.2 with σ_C gives t·μ₀(S_t) ≤ σ(E ∖ C). By Theorem 1.15(2) (sibling) for σ⌞E there are closed C_k ⊆ E with σ(E ∖ C_k) → 0, so μ₀(S_t) = 0; outside E ∪ U₀ ∪ ⋃_m S_{1/m} the quotient tends to 0.

I.5 (Lemma 3.19, Case 1) There is a Borel B with μ₀(B) = 0 such that μ(S ∖ B) = 0 whenever μ₀(S) = 0.
 Proof (printed). Let 𝒜 := {Borel A : μ₀(A) = 0}, α := sup{μ(A) : A ∈ 𝒜} ≤ μ(X) < ∞, and A_j ∈ 𝒜 with μ(A_j) → α; B := ⋃_j A_j ∈ 𝒜 and μ(B) = α. If μ₀(S) = 0, Borel regularity of μ₀ gives a Borel A ⊇ S with μ₀(A) = 0; A ∪ B ∈ 𝒜, so μ(S ∖ B) ≤ μ(A ∖ B) = μ(A ∪ B) − μ(B) ≤ α − α = 0.

I.6 μ̃ := μ⌞(X ∖ B) is Borel regular (I.0), finite, absolutely continuous with respect to μ₀ (μ₀(S) = 0 ⇒ μ̃(S) = μ(S ∖ B) = 0), and has the SVP: given A and a fine family on A, the SVP of μ₀ (μ₀(A) < ∞ in the finite case) gives a countable disjoint subfamily 𝓑' with μ₀(A ∖ ⋃𝓑') = 0, hence μ̃(A ∖ ⋃𝓑') = 0. The same argument shows: every finite Borel regular σ which is absolutely continuous with respect to μ₀ has the SVP.

I.7 (Theorem 3.21) Let σ be Borel regular with σ(X) < ∞, absolutely continuous with respect to μ₀, A ⊆ X, t > 0, and liminf_{ρ↓0} σ(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) ≤ t for all x ∈ A ∖ U₀. Then σ(A) ≤ t·μ₀(A).
 Proof (printed proof of 3.21(i), using the SVP of σ from I.6; this is also 3.21(ii) when σ = μ̃). σ(A ∩ U₀) = 0 because μ₀(U₀) = 0 and σ is absolutely continuous with respect to μ₀. Let A' := A ∖ U₀, so σ(A) = σ(A'). Let ϑ > t and ε > 0; by Theorem 1.15(1) (sibling) for μ₀ choose an open U ⊇ A with μ₀(U) < μ₀(A) + ε. The family {(x, ρ) : x ∈ A', ρ > 0, B_ρ(x) ⊆ U, σ(B_ρ(x)) < ϑμ₀(B_ρ(x))} is fine on A' (the quotient is < ϑ at arbitrarily small ρ, μ₀(B_ρ(x)) ∈ (0, ∞)). The SVP of σ gives countably many disjoint such balls B_j with σ(A' ∖ ⋃B_j) = 0, so σ(A') ≤ Σσ(B_j) ≤ ϑΣμ₀(B_j) = ϑμ₀(⋃B_j) ≤ ϑμ₀(U) ≤ ϑ(μ₀(A) + ε). Let ε → 0, ϑ ↓ t.

I.8 (the singular part has density 0) By I.4 with σ := μ⌞B (Borel regular, finite; B is σ-measurable) and E := B: for μ₀-a.e. x ∉ B — hence, as μ₀(B) = 0, for μ₀-a.e. x — s_x(ρ) := μ(B ∩ B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) → 0. Since B is μ-measurable, μ(B_ρ(x)) = μ̃(B_ρ(x)) + μ(B ∩ B_ρ(x)), so for x ∉ U₀: q_x(ρ) = q̃_x(ρ) + s_x(ρ) with q̃_x(ρ) := μ̃(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)). Hence for μ₀-a.e. x the limsup and liminf of q_x and of q̃_x coincide, q_x converges iff q̃_x does, and then with the same limit.

I.9 (Theorem 3.23(ii): existence and finiteness of the density) For rationals 0 < a < b let E_{a,b} := {x ∉ U₀ : liminf q̃_x < a < b < limsup q̃_x}. By I.2 (σ := μ̃), μ̃(E_{a,b}) ≥ b·μ₀(E_{a,b}); by I.7 (σ := μ̃), μ̃(E_{a,b}) ≤ a·μ₀(E_{a,b}). As μ₀(E_{a,b}) < ∞ and a < b, μ₀(E_{a,b}) = 0. So {x ∉ U₀ : liminf q̃_x < limsup q̃_x} = ⋃_{a<b} E_{a,b} is μ₀-null. Together with I.1, I.8 and I.3 there is a μ₀-null set S₁ such that for every x ∉ S₁: x ∉ U₀, q_x(ρ) converges as ρ ↓ 0, its limit is Θ(x) (a convergent function's limsup is its limit), and Θ(x) < ∞.

I.10 (measurability of Θ; printed measurability argument of 3.23) For ρ > 0, x ↦ μ(B_ρ(x)) is upper semicontinuous (if y_k → x, every point lying in infinitely many B_ρ(y_k) lies in B_ρ(x), so by the reverse Fatou inequality for the finite measure μ on M_μ, limsup_k μ(B_ρ(y_k)) ≤ μ(limsup_k B_ρ(y_k)) ≤ μ(B_ρ(x))), hence Borel; likewise x ↦ μ₀(B_ρ(x)). So g_i(x) := μ(B_{1/i}(x))/μ₀(B_{1/i}(x)) is Borel and G := limsup_i g_i is Borel. For x ∉ S₁, Θ(x) = lim_i g_i(x) = G(x). Choose a Borel S₂ ⊇ S₁ with μ₀(S₂) = 0. Then Θ = G off S₂, so Θ is μ₀-measurable ({Θ > c} differs from the Borel set {G > c} ∖ S₂ by a subset of the null set S₂), and Θ = G μ₀-a.e.
 The same facts I.1–I.10 hold with μ replaced by any finite Borel regular σ (with its own B, σ̃, S₁, Θ_σ).

I.11 (Theorem 3.24(i), finite case; printed proof) Let σ be Borel regular with σ(X) < ∞ and absolutely continuous with respect to μ₀, Θ_σ(x) := limsup_ρ σ(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)). Then σ(A) = ∫_A Θ_σ dμ₀ for every Borel A.
 Proof. By I.6 σ has the SVP, so I.7 applies to σ itself, and I.9–I.10 (for σ, where the decomposition set B_σ has σ(B_σ) = 0 by absolute continuity, so σ̃ = σ) give a μ₀-null set S_σ ⊇ U₀ off which the density lim_ρ σ(B_ρ(x))/μ₀(B_ρ(x)) exists, equals Θ_σ(x) and is finite; Θ_σ is μ₀-measurable. Put ν(A) := ∫_A Θ_σ dμ₀ for μ₀-measurable A. Every μ₀-measurable set M differs from a Borel set by a subset of a Borel μ₀-null set (Borel hulls of M and X ∖ M, μ₀ finite), which is σ-null; hence M is σ-measurable. Fix a Borel A and t > 1, and split A into the disjoint μ₀- (hence σ-) measurable pieces A ∩ S_σ, A⁰ := (A ∖ S_σ) ∩ {Θ_σ = 0}, and A_k := (A ∖ S_σ) ∩ {t^k ≤ Θ_σ < t^{k+1}}, k ∈ ℤ (they cover A since Θ_σ < ∞ off S_σ).
  • σ(A ∩ S_σ) = 0 = ν(A ∩ S_σ), since μ₀(S_σ) = 0.
  • On A⁰ the density exists and is 0, so its liminf is ≤ ε for every ε > 0; I.7 gives σ(A⁰) ≤ εμ₀(X) for all ε, so σ(A⁰) = 0 = ν(A⁰).
  • On A_k the density exists with value in [t^k, t^{k+1}), so limsup ≥ t^k and liminf ≤ t^{k+1}; I.2 and I.7 give t^k μ₀(A_k) ≤ σ(A_k) ≤ t^{k+1}μ₀(A_k), while t^kμ₀(A_k) ≤ ν(A_k) ≤ t^{k+1}μ₀(A_k). Hence σ(A_k) ≤ t·ν(A_k) and ν(A_k) ≤ t·σ(A_k).
 Summing over the pieces (countable additivity of σ on M_σ and of ν): σ(A) ≤ t·ν(A) and ν(A) ≤ t·σ(A) < ∞; letting t ↓ 1, σ(A) = ν(A). (Printed: “(a/b)ν(A_{a,b}) ≤ μ(A_{a,b}) ≤ (b/a)ν(A_{a,b}) and it follows that ν(A) = μ(A).”)

I.12 (Theorem 3.24(ii), finite case; printed “apply the previous argument to μ⌞(X ∖ B)”) By I.11 with σ := μ̃ (I.6), μ̃(A) = ∫_A Θ̃ dμ₀ for Borel A, where Θ̃ := limsup q̃. By I.8–I.9, Θ̃ = Θ μ₀-a.e., and both are μ₀-measurable (I.10), so ∫_A Θ̃ dμ₀ = ∫_A Θ dμ₀. As B is Borel, μ(A) = μ(A ∖ B) + μ(A ∩ B) = μ̃(A) + μ(B ∩ A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(B ∩ A). So (ii) holds with Z := B.

PART II. THE GENERAL CASE (printed: “Since μ, μ₀ are open σ-finite, we can assume μ(X) < ∞, μ₀(X) < ∞”; the reduction is made explicit).

II.1 Let (V_j) and (V'_k) be the open covers witnessing open σ-finiteness of μ and μ₀, and let (W_m)_{m≥1} enumerate the open sets V_j ∩ V'_k; then X = ⋃_m W_m and μ(W_m), μ₀(W_m) < ∞. Put μ_m := μ⌞W_m, μ₀_m := μ₀⌞W_m (Borel regular by I.0, finite), and W'_m := W_m ∖ ⋃_{l<m} W_l (Borel, pairwise disjoint, ⋃_m W'_m = X). μ₀_m has the SVP: for A with μ₀(A ∩ W_m) < ∞ and a family fine on A, the pairs centred in A ∩ W_m form a family fine on A ∩ W_m, and the SVP of μ₀ gives a countable disjoint subfamily 𝓑' with μ₀_m(A ∖ ⋃𝓑') = μ₀((A ∩ W_m) ∖ ⋃𝓑') = 0. Likewise μ_m has the SVP if μ has. For x ∈ W_m and ρ small (B_ρ(x) ⊆ W_m), μ_m(B_ρ(x)) = μ(B_ρ(x)) and μ₀_m(B_ρ(x)) = μ₀(B_ρ(x)); so the quotients for (μ_m, μ₀_m) and (μ, μ₀) coincide for small ρ, and at x ∈ W_m the upper and lower densities, the existence of the limit and its value are the same for both pairs; in particular Θ_m = Θ on W_m (Θ_m the upper density of μ_m w.r.t. μ₀_m). A set N ⊆ W_m is μ₀-null iff μ₀_m-null; on μ₀-measurable subsets of W_m the measures μ₀_m and μ₀ agree, so ∫_E g dμ₀_m = ∫_E g dμ₀ for μ₀-measurable g ≥ 0 and μ₀-measurable E ⊆ W_m.

II.2 Clause (0). For each m, I.9 for (μ_m, μ₀_m) gives a μ₀_m-null N_m off which the quotient for (μ_m, μ₀_m) converges to Θ_m. For x ∈ W_m ∖ N_m, q_x(ρ) converges to Θ(x) by II.1. The exceptional set is contained in ⋃_m (N_m ∩ W_m), which is μ₀-null. This is `∀ᵐ x ∂μ₀, Tendsto q_x (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 (Θ x))`. Moreover Θ is μ₀-measurable: on each W'_m it equals Θ_m, which is μ₀_m-measurable by I.10, and a subset of W_m which is μ₀_m-measurable is μ₀-measurable (it is a Borel set up to a subset of a μ₀_m-null, hence μ₀-null, subset of W_m).

II.3 Clause (ii). For each m, I.12 for (μ_m, μ₀_m) gives a Borel Z_m with μ₀_m(Z_m) = 0 and μ_m(A) = ∫_A Θ_m dμ₀_m + μ_m(Z_m ∩ A) for all Borel A. Let Z := ⋃_m (Z_m ∩ W'_m), a Borel set with μ₀(Z) ≤ Σ_m μ₀(Z_m ∩ W_m) = Σ_m μ₀_m(Z_m) = 0. For a Borel A let A_m := A ∩ W'_m ⊆ W_m. By II.1 (Θ_m = Θ on W_m, Z_m ∩ A_m = Z ∩ A_m),
  μ(A_m) = μ_m(A_m) = ∫_{A_m} Θ_m dμ₀_m + μ_m(Z_m ∩ A_m) = ∫_{A_m} Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z ∩ A_m).
Summing over m (A and Z ∩ A are the disjoint unions of the Borel sets A_m, resp. Z ∩ A_m; countable additivity of μ on Borel sets and of the integral) gives μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z ∩ A).

II.4 Clause (i). If μ₀(E) = 0 ⇒ μ(E) = 0 for all E, then μ(Z ∩ A) = 0 for the Z of II.3 (as μ₀(Z ∩ A) = 0), so μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ for every Borel A.

II.5 Clause (iii) (printed proof of (iii): the density of μ is infinite exactly on the singular part). Assume μ also has the SVP; let Z be as in II.3.
 (a) μ₀(Z_∞) = 0: if q_x → ∞ then Θ(x) = ∞; for each m, Z_∞ ∩ W_m ⊆ {x ∈ W_m : Θ_m(x) = ∞}, which is μ₀_m-null by I.3; hence μ₀(Z_∞ ∩ W_m) = 0 for all m.
 (b) μ(Z ∖ Z_∞) = 0: fix m and n ∈ ℕ, and let E := (Z ∩ W_m) ∩ {x : Θ_*(x) < n}. Points x ∈ W_m ∩ U₀ with μ(B_ρ(x)) > 0 for all ρ have q_x(ρ) = ∞ for small ρ, hence Θ_*(x) = ∞ and x ∉ E; the set W_m ∩ {x : μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ} is μ-null (I.1 for μ_m, which has the SVP). Let E' := E ∖ (U₀ ∪ {x : μ(B_ρ(x)) = 0 for some ρ}). For ϑ > n and ε > 0 choose (Theorem 1.15(1) for μ₀_m) an open U ⊇ E' with μ₀_m(U) < μ₀_m(E') + ε = ε (μ₀(E') ≤ μ₀(Z) = 0). The pairs (x, ρ), x ∈ E', B_ρ(x) ⊆ U ∩ W_m, μ(B_ρ(x)) < ϑμ₀(B_ρ(x)), form a family fine on E'; the SVP of μ_m gives disjoint such balls B_j with μ_m(E' ∖ ⋃B_j) = 0, so μ(E') = μ_m(E') ≤ Σμ(B_j) ≤ ϑΣμ₀(B_j) ≤ ϑμ₀_m(U) ≤ ϑε. Hence μ(E') = 0 and μ(E) = 0. Taking the union over m and n: μ-a.e. x ∈ Z has Θ_*(x) = ∞, i.e. q_x(ρ) → ∞, i.e. x ∈ Z_∞.
 (c) μ(Z_∞ ∖ Z) = 0: choose a Borel H ⊇ Z_∞ with μ₀(H) = 0; by (ii) applied to the Borel set H ∖ Z, μ(H ∖ Z) = ∫_{H∖Z} Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z ∩ (H ∖ Z)) = 0 + 0, and Z_∞ ∖ Z ⊆ H ∖ Z.
 (d) For Borel A: μ(Z_∞ ∩ A) ≤ μ(Z ∩ A) + μ(Z_∞ ∖ Z) = μ(Z ∩ A) and μ(Z ∩ A) ≤ μ(Z_∞ ∩ A) + μ(Z ∖ Z_∞) = μ(Z_∞ ∩ A). So μ(A) = ∫_A Θ dμ₀ + μ(Z_∞ ∩ A) by (ii).
This proves (0), (i), (ii), (iii). ∎

Formalization note (non-binding): `Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.simon_theorem_3_23_ii` (Chapter01/RadonNikodymDensity.lean) gives clause (0) outside a Borel μ₀-null set; `simon_theorem_3_24_i`, `simon_theorem_3_24_ii`, `simon_theorem_3_24_iii` (Chapter01/RadonNikodymTheorem.lean, with the local instance `MeasurableSpace X := borel X`) give (i)–(iii) with integrals against `hμ₀.toBorelMeasure` and `OuterMeasure.restrict Z μ` (= μ(A ∩ Z)); `outerInfiniteDensitySet μ μ₀` is literally Z_∞. Transport the lintegrals to `caratheodoryMeasure μ₀` via `setLIntegral_trim_ae` with `(caratheodoryMeasure μ₀).trim _ = hμ₀.toBorelMeasure`, using that Θ is a.e. equal to the Borel `rnDeriv` (`ae_outerRelativeUpperDensity_eq_rnDeriv`, `Measure.measurable_rnDeriv`).
proof_key_steps: Finite case: U₀ is μ₀-null; 3.13 (upper comparison); 3.14 (Θ < ∞ μ₀-a.e.); 3.15 (densities of finite measures vanish off measurable sets).
Lemma 3.19: a Borel μ₀-null B with μ⌞(X ∖ B) ≪ μ₀; μ̃ := μ⌞(X ∖ B) and every finite σ ≪ μ₀ inherit the Symmetric Vitali Property.
3.21: lower comparison σ(A) ≤ t·μ₀(A) for such σ.
The singular part μ⌞B has density 0 μ₀-a.e., so the quotients of μ and μ̃ have the same limits.
3.23: the sets E_{a,b} are μ₀-null by 3.13 and 3.21, so the density exists, equals Θ and is finite μ₀-a.e.; Θ is μ₀-measurable (upper semicontinuity of ball measures).
3.24(i), finite case: σ ≪ μ₀ ⇒ σ(A) = ∫_A Θ_σ dμ₀ by t-adic slicing with 3.13 and 3.21; (ii), finite case, with Z = B by applying (i) to μ̃.
General case: localize to W_m = V_j ∩ V'_k; clause (0) and (ii) glue over the disjoint Borel pieces W'_m; (i) follows from (ii).
(iii): μ₀(Z_∞) = 0 by 3.14; μ(Z ∖ Z_∞) = 0 by a 3.21-type argument with the Vitali property of μ; μ(Z_∞ ∖ Z) = 0 by (ii); hence μ(Z_∞ ∩ A) = μ(Z ∩ A).

subproblems.title: Density bounds for Hausdorff measure (Simon 3.26, with 2.4–2.6)
subproblems.statement: For every metric space X, real n ≥ 0 and Hⁿ-measurable A ⊆ X: (1) if Hⁿ(A) < ∞ then Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ, A, x) ≤ 1 for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ A; (2) if Hⁿ_δ(A) < ∞ for every real δ > 0 then Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ_∞, A, x) ≥ 2^{−n} for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ A.
subproblems.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `HausdorffDensityBounds` (Simon, Ch. 1, (2.4)–(2.6) and Theorem 3.26; printed proofs, transcribed and completed).

Statement. Let (X, d) be a metric space, n ≥ 0 real, and A ⊆ X an Hⁿ-measurable set.
 (1) If Hⁿ(A) < ∞, then Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ, A, x) ≤ 1 for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ A.
 (2) If Hⁿ_δ(A) < ∞ for every real δ > 0, then Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ_∞, A, x) ≥ 2^{−n} for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ A.

Conventions. For δ ∈ (0, ∞], Hⁿ_δ(∅) = 0 and, for nonempty E, Hⁿ_δ(E) = ω_n inf{Σ_j (diam C_j/2)ⁿ : E ⊆ ⋃_j C_j countable, diam C_j < δ} (2.2) (empty C_j contribute 0; inf ∅ = ∞; ω_n = π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2+1) > 0; x⁰ = 1). Hⁿ_δ is an outer measure, non-increasing in δ, Hⁿ_∞ ≤ Hⁿ_δ, and Hⁿ = sup_{δ>0} Hⁿ_δ = lim_{δ↓0} Hⁿ_δ (2.1) (including δ = ∞ in the supremum changes nothing). Θ^{*n}(σ, A, x) := limsup_{ρ↓0} σ(A ∩ B_ρ(x))/(ω_n ρⁿ) (3.1), B_ρ(x) the closed ball. “P for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ A” means Hⁿ({x ∈ A : not P(x)}) = 0.

Dependencies. Theorem 1.13 = sibling `caratheodory_criterion`; Theorem 1.15 = sibling `borel_regular_approximation`; Theorem 3.3 = first conjunct of sibling `upper_density_comparison_and_theorem`.

STEP 1 ((2.4), (2.5)). If E, F ⊆ X and r > 0 with d(e, f) ≥ r for all e ∈ E, f ∈ F, then Hⁿ_δ(E ∪ F) = Hⁿ_δ(E) + Hⁿ_δ(F) for every δ ∈ (0, r], hence Hⁿ(E ∪ F) = Hⁿ(E) + Hⁿ(F).
 Proof. “≤” is subadditivity. For “≥” we may assume Hⁿ_δ(E ∪ F) < ∞. Let {C_j} be a countable cover of E ∪ F with diam C_j < δ ≤ r. No C_j meets both E and F. The C_j meeting E cover E and the C_j meeting F cover F, with disjoint sets of indices, so ω_nΣ_j(diam C_j/2)ⁿ ≥ Hⁿ_δ(E) + Hⁿ_δ(F). Take the infimum over covers; then let δ ↓ 0.

STEP 2 ((2.6): Hⁿ is Borel regular).
 (a) By Step 1 and Carathéodory's criterion (sibling `caratheodory_criterion`, applied to the outer measure Hⁿ on X), every Borel set is Hⁿ-measurable.
 (b) Borel hulls (using Remark 2.3(1): diam C̄ = diam C, so in (2.2) the C_j may be taken closed). Let E ⊆ X. If Hⁿ(E) = ∞ take X. Otherwise, for each k ≥ 1, Hⁿ_{1/k}(E) ≤ Hⁿ(E) < ∞, so there is a countable cover {C_{kj}}_j of E by closed sets with diam C_{kj} < 1/k and ω_nΣ_j(diam C_{kj}/2)ⁿ < Hⁿ_{1/k}(E) + 1/k. G := ⋂_k ⋃_j C_{kj} is Borel and contains E. For m ≤ k, Hⁿ_{1/m}(G) ≤ Hⁿ_{1/k}(G) ≤ ω_nΣ_j(diam C_{kj}/2)ⁿ < Hⁿ_{1/k}(E) + 1/k ≤ Hⁿ(E) + 1/k; letting k → ∞ and then m → ∞, Hⁿ(G) ≤ Hⁿ(E); the reverse inequality is monotonicity.

STEP 3 (remarks after (1.12)). If A is Hⁿ-measurable with Hⁿ(A) < ∞, then σ := Hⁿ⌞A (σ(S) = Hⁿ(A ∩ S)) is Borel regular and finite. [Hⁿ-measurable sets are σ-measurable: σ(S) = Hⁿ(S∩A∩E) + Hⁿ((S∩A)∖E). Hulls: by Step 2 take Borel B₁ ⊇ A with Hⁿ(B₁) = Hⁿ(A), so Hⁿ(B₁ ∖ A) = 0, and Borel B₂ ⊇ B₁ ∖ A with Hⁿ(B₂) = 0; for S take Borel B₃ ⊇ S ∩ A with Hⁿ(B₃) = Hⁿ(S ∩ A); B := B₃ ∪ (X ∖ B₁) ∪ B₂ ⊇ S is Borel and σ(B) ≤ Hⁿ(B₃) + Hⁿ(A ∖ B₁) + Hⁿ(B₂) = σ(S).] Being finite, σ is open σ-finite (V_n := X); and in a metric space every closed set C (C ≠ ∅) is ⋂_k {x : dist(x, C) < 1/k}, a countable intersection of open sets.

STEP 4 (proof of (1); printed). Assume Hⁿ(A) < ∞; σ := Hⁿ⌞A as in Step 3. Let t > 1, ε > 0, and A_t := {x ∈ A : Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ, A, x) ≥ t}. By Theorem 1.15(1) (sibling) for σ, σ(A_t) = inf{σ(U) : U ⊇ A_t open}, so there is an open U ⊇ A_t with Hⁿ(A ∩ U) = σ(U) < σ(A_t) + ε = Hⁿ(A_t) + ε. For x ∈ A_t ⊆ U we have B_ρ(x) ⊆ U for small ρ, so σ((A ∩ U) ∩ B_ρ(x)) = Hⁿ(A ∩ B_ρ(x)) for small ρ and Θ^{*n}(σ, A ∩ U, x) = Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ, A, x) ≥ t. Theorem 3.3 (sibling) applied to the Borel regular σ with A₁ := A_t ⊆ A₂ := A ∩ U gives
  t·Hⁿ(A_t) ≤ σ(A ∩ U) = Hⁿ(A ∩ U) < Hⁿ(A_t) + ε.
Letting ε → 0, t·Hⁿ(A_t) ≤ Hⁿ(A_t) ≤ Hⁿ(A) < ∞, so Hⁿ(A_t) = 0 since t > 1. Finally {x ∈ A : Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ, A, x) > 1} = ⋃_k A_{1+1/k} is Hⁿ-null, which is (1).

STEP 5 (proof of (2)). The printed argument is completed below; the measurability of A is not needed. Write Θ_∞(x) := Θ^{*n}(Hⁿ_∞, A, x).
 5.0 (n = 0.) For x ∈ A and ρ > 0 the set A ∩ B_ρ(x) contains x, so every cover of it contains a nonempty set, which costs (diam/2)⁰ = 1; hence H⁰_∞(A ∩ B_ρ(x)) ≥ ω_0 = 1 = ω_0ρ⁰ and Θ_∞(x) ≥ 1 = 2^{−0} for every x ∈ A. From now on n > 0.
 5.1 (Lemma.) If E ⊆ X and diam E < δ < ∞, then Hⁿ_δ(E) = Hⁿ_∞(E). [Hⁿ_∞ ≤ Hⁿ_δ always. Conversely, if {D_i} is a cover of E admissible for Hⁿ_∞, then {D_i ∩ E} covers E, diam(D_i ∩ E) ≤ min(diam D_i, diam E) < δ, and its cost is not larger.]
 5.2 For j ≥ 1 let B_j := {x ∈ A : Hⁿ_∞(A ∩ B_ρ(x)) ≤ (1 − 1/j)2^{−n}ω_nρⁿ for all ρ ∈ (0, 1/j)}. If x ∈ A and Θ_∞(x) < 2^{−n}, pick c with Θ_∞(x) < c < 2^{−n}; then Hⁿ_∞(A ∩ B_ρ(x)) < cω_nρⁿ for all ρ ∈ (0, ρ₀) for some ρ₀ > 0, and choosing j with 1/j ≤ ρ₀ and (1 − 1/j)2^{−n} ≥ c gives x ∈ B_j. (This is the printed choice of δ_x ∈ (0, 1) and of B ⊆ B₀ with δ_x > 1/j.) So {x ∈ A : Θ_∞(x) < 2^{−n}} ⊆ ⋃_j B_j, and it suffices to prove Hⁿ(B_j) = 0 for each j.
 5.3 Fix j, put δ := 1/j and B := B_j, and let δ' ∈ (0, δ]. Let {C_i} be any countable cover of B with diam C_i < δ'; discarding the C_i that miss B (this lowers the cost and keeps a cover) we may assume C_i ∩ B ≠ ∅; pick x_i ∈ C_i ∩ B and let r_i := diam C_i < δ'. Every point of C_i is within r_i of x_i, and B ⊆ A, so B ∩ C_i ⊆ A ∩ B_{r_i}(x_i).
  • If r_i > 0: diam(B ∩ C_i) ≤ r_i < δ', so by 5.1 and the definition of B (x_i ∈ B, 0 < r_i < δ' ≤ δ),
    Hⁿ_{δ'}(B ∩ C_i) = Hⁿ_∞(B ∩ C_i) ≤ Hⁿ_∞(A ∩ B_{r_i}(x_i)) ≤ (1 − δ)2^{−n}ω_n r_iⁿ = (1 − δ)ω_n(diam C_i/2)ⁿ.
  • If r_i = 0: B ∩ C_i = {x_i}, and Hⁿ_{δ'}({x_i}) = 0 = (1 − δ)ω_n(diam C_i/2)ⁿ (the one-point cover costs ω_n0ⁿ = 0 as n > 0).
  Hence Hⁿ_{δ'}(B) ≤ Σ_i Hⁿ_{δ'}(B ∩ C_i) ≤ (1 − δ)ω_nΣ_i(diam C_i/2)ⁿ. Taking the infimum over all such covers, Hⁿ_{δ'}(B) ≤ (1 − δ)Hⁿ_{δ'}(B). Since Hⁿ_{δ'}(B) ≤ Hⁿ_{δ'}(A) < ∞ by hypothesis and 1 − δ < 1, Hⁿ_{δ'}(B) = 0. As δ' ∈ (0, δ] was arbitrary, Hⁿ(B) = sup_{0<δ'≤δ}Hⁿ_{δ'}(B) = 0.
